book_skeleton.subject: physics

chapters.title: Describing Motion Around Us
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces the study of motion in nature, examining the wide variety of motions through idealised forms such as linear, circular, and oscillatory. It deepens the understanding of linear motion (motion in a straight line) and uniform circular motion, extending earlier concepts of distance, time, and speed.

book_skeleton.subject_overview: This textbook explores the physics of motion in the natural world, building on earlier concepts of distance, time and speed. It focuses on idealised forms of motion such as linear, circular, and oscillatory motion. The material is designed to help students study complex real-world motions through simplified scientific models.

chapters.title: Describing Motion Around Us
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces the study of motion in nature, examining the wide variety of motions through idealised forms such as linear, circular, and oscillatory. It deepens the understanding of linear motion (motion in a straight line) and uniform circular motion, extending earlier concepts of distance, time, and speed.

events.text: Linear motion = motion along one straight line, forward or backward only
Position = where the object is on the line
To describe motion, first describe position at each instant of time
Position = reference point + distance + direction
position changes in time means motion
Distance = total path covered. Displacement = straight-line change in position, with direction.
If she'd returned all the way to O, displacement = 0
velocity = displacement over time
Back to start means zero displacement, so zero average velocity
change in velocity over time taken
a equals change in velocity divided by time
Q: Find the average acceleration when the accelerator is pressed, and when the brakes are pressed.
Part (i): u = 10 m/s, v = 15 m/s, t = 10 s
a = (15 - 10) / 10 = 5 / 10 = 0.5 m/s^2, along velocity
Part (ii): u = 15 m/s, v = 0 m/s, t = 5 s
a = (0 - 15) / 5 = -15 / 5 = -3 m/s^2, opposite to velocity
(i) a = 0.5 m/s^2 (along velocity); (ii) a = -3 m/s^2 (opposite velocity)
Q: A falling object has velocity 9.8, 19.6, 29.4, 39.2 m/s at t = 1, 2, 3, 4 s. Find the average acceleration in each interval.
Average acceleration = 9.8 m/s^2, constant, in the direction of motion (g, due to gravity)
Steady motion = straight rising line
Steeper line means moving faster
Q: An object dropped from a height — find how its velocity changes each second.
At t = 0 s, v = 0 m/s
At t = 1 s, v = 9.8 m/s
At t = 2 s, v = 19.6 m/s
At t = 3 s, v = 29.4 m/s
At t = 4 s, v = 39.2 m/s
Velocity increases by 9.8 m/s every second → acceleration is constant
Slope of position-time graph = speed
Time on X-axis, position on Y-axis
Go across to the time, then up to the position
Each table row becomes one point: across to the time, up to the position
Q: Plot the position-time graph for a vehicle: (0s, 0m), (1s, 20m), (2s, 40m), (3s, 60m), (4s, 80m), (5s, 100m), (6s, 120m)
Axes: time on X-axis, position on Y-axis
Scale: X-axis 5 divisions = 1 s; Y-axis 5 divisions = 20 m
At 0 s, position 0 m → plot at the origin
At 1 s, draw line parallel to Y-axis; from 20 m, line parallel to X-axis; intersection = point (1 s, 20 m)
Similarly plot (2s,40m), (3s,60m), (4s,80m), (5s,100m), (6s,120m); connect all points
The position-time graph is a straight line (constant-speed motion)
Q: Plot position-time graph for a vehicle starting from rest and speeding up
X-axis: 5 divisions = 2 seconds
Y-axis: 5 divisions = 5 meters
Points do NOT lie on a straight line
The points form a curve, not a straight line
Straight line drawn
Slope of position-time graph equals velocity
Flat line means steady velocity
Slope of v-t graph = acceleration
Q: A car moves in a straight line at a steady velocity of 72 km/h (20 m/s). What does its velocity-time graph look like?
Velocity stays fixed at 20 m/s for all time t
Graph: horizontal line at v = 20 m/s
A horizontal line at 20 m/s (72 km/h), constant velocity, zero acceleration
Q: A car starts from rest; velocity rises 0, 2.5, 5.0, 7.5, 10.0, 12.5, 15.0 m/s at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 s. Describe its v-t graph.
Every 5 s, velocity rises by a fixed 2.5 m/s
Constant acceleration — the v-t graph is an upward straight line
Q: A car slows from 15.0 m/s; plot its velocity-time graph and find the acceleration.
Each 5 s interval: velocity drops by 2.5 m/s
Acceleration = -0.5 m/s^2 (constant, straight downward line)
Q: Find the average acceleration between 10 s and 20 s, where v = 5 m/s at 10 s and v = 10 m/s at 20 s
a = 5 m/s / 10 s
a = 0.5 m/s² (meters per second squared)
Q: Find the average acceleration from the velocity-time graph in Fig. 4.17e (same as Fig. 4.17c).
Average acceleration = slope of the v-t graph = -0.5 m/s^2
Average acceleration = -0.5 m/s^2 (acceleration opposes velocity; object slows down)
Q: Find the displacement for constant velocity 20 m/s over 6 s using the v-t graph
Area under v-t graph = rectangle (height = velocity, width = time)
Displacement = area = velocity x time
Displacement = 20 m/s x 6 s
Displacement = 120 meters
Q: Find the displacement from 10 s to 20 s on the velocity-time graph (region ABDE).
displacement = area of rectangle ACDE + area of triangle ABC
rectangle = 5 m/s times 10 s = 50 m
triangle = one half times 10 s times 5 m/s = 25 m
displacement = 50 m + 25 m = 75 m
Area under v-t graph = distance
Constant acceleration means a straight v-t line; its slope is a
a equals (v minus u) divided by t
Area under a v-t graph equals displacement
s equals u t plus one half a t squared
Motion in a plane = two independent straight-line motions at once
Across: steady. Up-down: gravity. Combine into the arc.
One full lap: distance equals two pi R, displacement equals zero
uniform = constant speed
Q: Object goes once around a circle of radius R in time T. Find average speed and average velocity.
Distance in one revolution = circumference = 2 pi R
Displacement after one revolution = 0
Average speed = 2 pi R / T ; Average velocity = 0
Constant speed, changing velocity, because direction changes

chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1:straight_line_track>> A ball dropped from your hand, a train on a track, a swimmer racing across a pool — what do all three secretly have in common? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Every single one of them moves <<TRACE:motion-line>> along a straight path — no curving, no swerving, just a clean line from here to there. <<SECTION:Motion in a Straight Line|id=sec-1>> Let me <<FOCUS:moving-object>> put one object on that line, and notice it can only do two things. It can <<FOCUS:forward-arrow>> move forward, this way along the line. Or it can <<FOCUS:backward-arrow>> move backward, the other way. <<UNFOCUS>> That's it — there is no third option, because it's stuck on one single line. <<WRITE_KEY:Linear motion = motion along one straight line, forward or backward only|id=key-1>> This is what we call linear motion, or motion in a straight line — and because there are no turns to worry about, it is the simplest kind of motion there is. <<PAUSE:short>> And that simplicity is exactly why we begin here — master the straight line, and curves and turns become just straight lines stitched together later. <<PAUSE:short>> Now here's a fair question: if the object is just sliding along this line, how would I actually describe where it is at any moment? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Position = where the object is on the line|id=text-1>> I drop a marker right where it sits — <<FOCUS:position-marker>> that single dot on the line tells me its position at this instant of time. <<WRITE_KEY:To describe motion, first describe position at each instant of time|id=key-2>> So before we can talk about how fast or how far, we must first be able to <<FOCUS:position-label>> state the object's position at each instant of time. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> That one idea — pinning down position instant by instant — is the foundation everything else about motion is built on. <<PAUSE:short>> So remember the two takeaways: straight-line motion is the simplest motion, forward or backward only — and to describe it, you start by describing position. Next, we'll do exactly that.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_1>>
If I tell you a treasure is buried twenty meters away, could you find it? Twenty meters from what? And in which direction? You'd be digging forever. <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_1:athlete_track_line>> <<SECTION:Describing Position|id=sec-1>> The problem is that distance alone floats in empty space. To pin anything down, we first plant a flag: a single fixed point that everyone agrees to measure from. We call that flag the reference point, and <<FOCUS:origin-point+origin-label>> here it sits at O, the starting line of a running track, which we call zero meters. <<PAUSE:short>> Now we <<TRACE:distance-scale>> lay down a measuring line from O so every spot on the track has a number: twenty meters, forty meters, sixty meters, and so on. <<UNFOCUS>> But is a number enough? If I say the runner is at sixty meters, have I really told you where she is? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Not quite, because sixty meters could be to the left or to the right. So we also <<FOCUS:direction-arrow>> fix a direction with this arrow, pointing forward along the track. <<WRITE_KEY:Position = reference point + distance + direction|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So a position is three things together: a fixed reference point, a distance from it, and a direction. <<PAUSE:short>> Watch the runner. At one instant she is here, <<FOCUS:position-b+b-label>> at point B, twenty meters from O along the track. A few seconds later she is here, <<FOCUS:position-a+a-label>> at point A, sixty meters from O. <<UNFOCUS>> Her position, measured from our flag, has changed. <<WRITE_TEXT:position changes in time means motion|id=text-1>> And that is exactly what motion is: when an object's position relative to the reference point changes as time passes, we say it is moving. <<PAUSE:short>> Flip it around: if her position from O never changed, instant after instant, she would be standing still, at rest. <<PAUSE:short>> So next time someone says something is twenty meters away, ask them the two questions that turn a useless number into a real location: from where, and which way?

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_2>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_2:athlete_track>> An athlete runs one hundred sixty meters around a track and ends up only forty meters from where she started. So how far did she travel — one hundred sixty, or forty? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:track-line>> Here's the track. She starts at this point, <<FOCUS:point-o>> which we'll call O, at the zero-meter mark. <<SECTION:Distance travelled|id=sec-1>> She runs forward, <<FOCUS:point-b>> past point B, <<FOCUS:point-a>> all the way to point A at the one-hundred-meter mark. Watch her feet <<TRACE:path-out>> cover that ground. Then she turns around and <<TRACE:path-back>> runs back from A to B, covering another sixty meters of ground. <<WRITE_EQUATION:160 = 100 + 60|id=eq-dist>> Add up <<FOCUS:path-out+path-back>> every bit of path her feet touched: one hundred plus sixty is one hundred sixty meters. <<UNFOCUS>> That total ground covered is the distance travelled, and it doesn't care which direction she went. <<PAUSE:short>> Now I'm going to ask a completely different question. Forget the path. Where did she start, and where did she actually end up? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> She started at O and finished at B. So the only thing that matters now is <<FOCUS:displacement-arrow>> this straight gap between start and finish. <<SECTION:Displacement|id=sec-2>> That straight-line change in position is forty meters, pointing forward. <<UNFOCUS>> We call it the displacement. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Distance = total path covered. Displacement = straight-line change in position, with direction.|id=key-1>> So distance travelled is the <<FOCUS:path-out+path-back>> total ground covered along the path, but displacement is the <<FOCUS:displacement-arrow>> straight-line change in position from start to finish — and displacement has a direction. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And here's the catch that trips everyone up: distance is just a single number, but displacement always needs two things — a size and a direction. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:If she'd returned all the way to O, displacement = 0|id=text-1>> Imagine she'd run all the way back to O. The distance travelled would be even bigger, but the displacement would be zero — she'd be exactly where she began. So next time someone says how far did you go, ask them which they mean — the ground you covered, or how far you ended up from the start. They're rarely the same number.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_3>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_3:track_journey>> If you walk all the way around a running track and end up exactly where you started, your average speed is big, but your average velocity is zero. How can both be true at once? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Speed versus velocity|id=sec-1>> You already know average speed. It just tells us how fast something moves, and we get it by dividing the total distance travelled by the time taken. Here is the key: <<FOCUS:path-curve>> distance is just a length, a plain number with no direction at all. <<UNFOCUS>> So average speed, built only from distance, is also just a number with no direction. <<PAUSE:short>> Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the time taken. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{average speed} = \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{time}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now look at <<TRACE:displacement-arrow>> this short straight arrow from where you started to where you finished. That straight-line shortcut, with its direction, is the displacement. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:velocity = displacement over time|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Average velocity is displacement divided by time. Because displacement carries a direction, average velocity carries a direction too. <<PAUSE:short>> Average velocity is the displacement divided by the time taken, and it points in the direction of the displacement. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{average velocity} = \dfrac{\text{displacement}}{\text{time}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> So back to our puzzle. You ran <<FOCUS:path-curve>> the whole long way around, building up a real total distance, so your average speed was clearly large. <<UNFOCUS>> But what happens to the displacement when you finish exactly where you began? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Back to start means zero displacement, so zero average velocity|id=key-1>> The start and the end <<FOCUS:start-point+end-point>> are the same spot, so the straight-line displacement shrinks to nothing. <<UNFOCUS>> Zero displacement means zero average velocity, even though you sprinted the whole way. <<PAUSE:short>> That is the whole idea. <<FOCUS:path-curve>> The winding distance feeds the speed; <<FOCUS:displacement-arrow>> the straight arrow feeds the velocity. <<UNFOCUS>> Same journey, two very different answers. And one last thing about steadiness. If something travels equal distances in every equal slice of time, that is uniform motion and the speed stays constant. Unequal distances mean it is speeding up or slowing down.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_4>>
Why does your body lurch forward the instant a bus slams its brakes, even though nothing actually pushed you? <<PAUSE:long>> That jolt you feel is your body sensing something change very fast: its velocity. One moment you were moving, the next you nearly weren't. <<PAUSE:short>> The physics word for how quickly velocity changes is acceleration. The bigger the jolt, the more violent the acceleration. <<SECTION:Average acceleration|id=sec-1>> So here is the heart of it: average acceleration is just how much the velocity changed, divided by how long it took to change. <<PAUSE:short>> Change in velocity means the velocity you ended with minus the velocity you started with. If you started at rest and ended fast, that change is large. <<WRITE_TEXT:change in velocity over time taken|id=text-1>> Now squeeze that big change into a tiny time, and you get a huge acceleration. Squeeze it into a long time, and the acceleration is gentle. <<WRITE_KEY:a equals change in velocity divided by time|id=key-1>> In plain words: take the final velocity, subtract the initial velocity, then divide by the time interval. That single number is the average acceleration. <<PAUSE:short>> Average acceleration is the final velocity minus the initial velocity, all divided by the time taken for that change. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a = \dfrac{v - u}{t_2 - t_1}|id=eq-1|boxed>> And because we divide a velocity, in meters per second, by a time in seconds, the unit comes out as meters per second squared. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_4:accel_direction_pair>> <<SECTION:Acceleration has direction|id=sec-2>> But here is the part people forget: acceleration is not just a number, it has a direction, just like velocity. When you are speeding up, the acceleration <<FOCUS:velocity-speeding+accel-speeding>> points the same way you are moving. <<UNFOCUS>> Velocity and acceleration march together. <<PAUSE:short>> So when does the acceleration <<FOCUS:velocity-slowing+accel-slowing>> point backwards, against your motion? <<UNFOCUS>> Think about that braking bus. <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. A bus is moving on a long straight highway. First, the driver presses the accelerator for ten seconds, and the velocity rises from thirty-six kilometers per hour, which is ten meters per second, up to fifty-four kilometers per hour, which is fifteen meters per second. Then later, the driver presses the brakes and the bus comes to a stop in five seconds. We want the average acceleration in both intervals. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the average acceleration when the accelerator is pressed, and when the brakes are pressed.|id=ex-q-1>> Let's handle part one, when the accelerator is pressed. Here the initial velocity u is ten meters per second, the final velocity v is fifteen meters per second, and the time t is ten seconds. Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by time. <<WRITE_STEP:Part (i): u = 10 m/s, v = 15 m/s, t = 10 s|id=ex-step-1>> So a equals fifteen meters per second minus ten meters per second, all divided by ten seconds. That gives five meters per second over ten seconds, which is zero point five meters per second squared. Since the magnitude of the velocity is increasing, this acceleration acts <<FOCUS:velocity-speeding+accel-speeding>> in the direction of the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (15 - 10) / 10 = 5 / 10 = 0.5 m/s^2, along velocity|id=ex-step-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now part two, when the brakes are pressed. Here the initial velocity u is fifty-four kilometers per hour, which is fifteen meters per second, the final velocity v is zero meters per second, and the time t is five seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:Part (ii): u = 15 m/s, v = 0 m/s, t = 5 s|id=ex-step-3>> So a equals zero meters per second minus fifteen meters per second, all over five seconds. That's negative fifteen meters per second divided by five seconds, which is negative three meters per second squared. The minus sign tells us the acceleration <<FOCUS:velocity-slowing+accel-slowing>> acts opposite to the direction of velocity, because the bus is slowing down. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (0 - 15) / 5 = -15 / 5 = -3 m/s^2, opposite to velocity|id=ex-step-4>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the two answers are: zero point five meters per second squared in the direction of velocity when accelerating, and negative three meters per second squared, opposite to velocity, when braking. <<WRITE_ANSWER:(i) a = 0.5 m/s^2 (along velocity); (ii) a = -3 m/s^2 (opposite velocity)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. An object is dropped from a height and falls straight down along a vertical path. As it comes down, its velocity keeps increasing: at one second the velocity is nine point eight meters per second, at two seconds it's nineteen point six meters per second, at three seconds it's twenty-nine point four meters per second, and at four seconds it's thirty-nine point two meters per second. We want to find the magnitude of the average acceleration in every successive one-second interval. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A falling object has velocity 9.8, 19.6, 29.4, 39.2 m/s at t = 1, 2, 3, 4 s. Find the average acceleration in each interval.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the first interval, between zero seconds and one second. Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the change in time. So that's nine point eight minus zero meters per second, over one minus zero seconds, which gives nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 0 to 1 s: a = (9.8 - 0)/(1 - 0) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now the interval between one second and two seconds. The velocity goes from nine point eight to nineteen point six meters per second. So we take nineteen point six minus nine point eight, over two minus one seconds, and again we get nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 1 to 2 s: a = (19.6 - 9.8)/(2 - 1) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Continuing for the next two intervals: between two and three seconds, twenty-nine point four minus nineteen point six over one second is again nine point eight meters per second squared; and between three and four seconds, thirty-nine point two minus twenty-nine point four over one second is once more nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 2 to 3 s: a = (29.4 - 19.6)/(3 - 2) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 3 to 4 s: a = (39.2 - 29.4)/(4 - 3) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-4>> Notice that each one-second interval gives the same average acceleration of nine point eight meters per second squared, so the average acceleration is constant. And since the velocity is increasing in the direction of motion, the acceleration is in the direction of motion as well. This is the acceleration due to gravity, denoted by g, equal to nine point eight meters per second squared, directed downward in the direction of motion. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Average acceleration = 9.8 m/s^2, constant, in the direction of motion (g, due to gravity)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> When you slow down, the acceleration <<FOCUS:velocity-slowing+accel-slowing>> points opposite to your velocity, dragging your speed down. <<UNFOCUS>> That backwards-pointing acceleration is exactly what threw you forward in your seat. <<PAUSE:short>> So next time you feel that jolt, you will know: your body just measured an acceleration, and even felt which way it pointed.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_2>>
Two cars race away from a traffic light. Without a single calculation, can you say which one speeds up faster? You can — if you let them draw you a picture. <<PAUSE:long>> Up to now we've described motion with words and numbers: it moved ten meters, it took two seconds. True, but flat. <<SECTION:Why graph motion?|id=sec-1>> A graph gives us something better — a picture of the whole journey we can take in at a glance. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_2:position_time_graph>> Here's the trick. We pick two things that are connected — say, position and time — and we draw how one changes as the other changes. <<FOCUS:time-axis>> Time runs along the bottom, <<FOCUS:position-axis>> position climbs up the side. <<UNFOCUS>> Every dot on this picture answers one question: where was the object at this moment? Watch what happens when the object moves at a steady pace. The dots line up <<TRACE:steady-line>> into a straight, rising line. <<WRITE_TEXT:Steady motion = straight rising line|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And right there is the payoff: the whole story of the motion has become one picture you can read in a heartbeat — no calculation needed. <<PAUSE:short>> Now look closely at the line. Notice <<FOCUS:steady-line>> how steeply it climbs as we move to the right. <<UNFOCUS>> That steepness has a meaning. In the same slice of time, <<FOCUS:slope-marker>> a steeper line covers more position — and covering more distance in the same time is exactly what we mean by going faster. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So let's race the cars. <<TRACE:steep-line>> Here's a second line, climbing more steeply than the first. <<FOCUS:steep-line+steady-line>> Steeper line, faster car. <<UNFOCUS>> You read the answer straight off the picture — that's the power we were after. <<WRITE_KEY:Steeper line means moving faster|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> What about an object that's just sitting still — what would its line look like? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. An object is dropped from a height, and we track its velocity each second as it falls. At time zero seconds, its initial velocity is zero meters per second. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: An object dropped from a height — find how its velocity changes each second.|id=ex-q-1>> Now let's read off the velocity at each second. At one second the velocity is nine point eight meters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 0 s, v = 0 m/s|id=ex-step-1-1>> At two seconds it is nineteen point six meters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 1 s, v = 9.8 m/s|id=ex-step-1-2>> At three seconds it is twenty-nine point four meters per second, and at four seconds it is thirty-nine point two meters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 2 s, v = 19.6 m/s|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 3 s, v = 29.4 m/s|id=ex-step-1-4>> <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 4 s, v = 39.2 m/s|id=ex-step-1-5>> Notice that every second the velocity goes up by the same nine point eight meters per second. That equal jump each second means the acceleration is constant. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Velocity increases by 9.8 m/s every second → acceleration is constant|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Time keeps marching on, but position never changes — so <<FOCUS:flat-segment>> the line goes flat. <<UNFOCUS>> A horizontal line means standing still. The shape itself tells you the story. And that's the whole idea. <<WRITE_TEXT:Slope of position-time graph = speed|id=text-2>> A line that rises is moving, a steeper rise is faster, a flat line is at rest — the picture is the motion, made visible. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_2_1>>
Here's a table: at one second the car is at twenty meters, at two seconds forty meters, at three seconds sixty meters. Quick, without doing any maths, is it speeding up or slowing down? Hard to tell from a row of numbers, isn't it? <<PAUSE:long>> That's the whole problem with a table. The numbers are correct, but your eye can't see the story inside them. So let's turn that table into something you can read in one glance. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_2_1:position_time_axes>> <<SECTION:Building the axes|id=sec-1>> We start by drawing <<FOCUS:x-axis+y-axis>> two lines that cross at right angles. The corner where they meet has a name, <<FOCUS:origin>> the origin. The horizontal line is <<FOCUS:x-axis>> the X-axis, and along it we'll put time. The vertical line is <<FOCUS:y-axis>> the Y-axis, and up it we'll put position. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Time on X-axis, position on Y-axis|id=text-1>> Notice <<FOCUS:grid>> the faint squares, that's graph paper. <<UNFOCUS>> Each square is a fixed amount, so every point lands in exactly the right spot. Now, how does one row of the table become one dot on this grid? Take the row for two seconds and forty meters. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Go across to the time, then up to the position|id=step-1>> You go <<TRACE:trace-across>> across the X-axis until you reach two seconds, then you <<TRACE:trace-up>> travel straight up until you reach forty meters. Where those two meet, <<FOCUS:point-2s>> you put a dot. <<WRITE_KEY:Each table row becomes one point: across to the time, up to the position|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That single dot now carries both facts at once, the time and the position, locked into one spot on the picture. <<PAUSE:short>> Do that for every row of the table, and you get <<FOCUS:all-points>> a whole scatter of dots marching across the page. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And now look, the answer to my opening question is staring right at you. The dots climb in <<TRACE:all-points>> a perfectly straight, even line. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have data for a vehicle moving on a straight road. lecture_plan.chapter_arc: We begin with the simplest motion — a straight line — and build a precise language for it: position, displacement, velocity, acceleration. We then learn to SEE motion through graphs and capture it with equations, before stepping off the line into the plane to meet circular motion, where an object can move at constant speed yet never stop accelerating.
lecture_plan.opening_hook: Everything around you is moving — a falling ball, a car changing lanes, a child on a merry-go-round — yet we describe them all with just a handful of ideas. What are the words and pictures that let us pin down any motion in the universe?

coverage_checklist.description: Establish that motion needs a reference point and that position is measured from it
Sharply distinguish distance (scalar, path length) from displacement (vector, start-to-end) using a concrete there-and-back example
Distinguish speed from velocity and average from instantaneous, tying acceleration to the felt jolt of changing velocity
Show how to read slopes of position-time and velocity-time graphs as velocity and acceleration
State the three kinematic equations and connect them to constant acceleration
Make the case that uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity, hence acceleration even without speeding up
Tie the whole framework back to everyday motion (cars, falling balls, merry-go-rounds) so the abstractions feel real

lecture_plan.closing_summary: We started by asking what words and pictures let us pin down any motion around us — and now you have them. Position needs a reference point; displacement and velocity carry direction while distance and speed don't; acceleration measures how velocity changes. We turned all of this into graphs we can read at a glance and into three equations for constant acceleration. And when we left the straight line for the plane, we discovered something surprising: an object circling at constant speed is still accelerating, because its direction is forever changing. From a falling ball to a child on a merry-go-round, the same handful of ideas describes them all.

segments.narration_chapter: If I tell you a treasure is buried twenty meters away, could you find it? Twenty meters from what? And in which direction? You'd be digging forever. <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_1:athlete_track_line>> <<SECTION:Describing Position|id=sec-1>> The problem is that distance alone floats in empty space. To pin anything down, we first plant a flag: a single fixed point that everyone agrees to measure from. We call that flag the reference point, and <<FOCUS:origin-point+origin-label>> here it sits at O, the starting line of a running track, which we call zero meters. <<PAUSE:short>> Now we <<TRACE:distance-scale>> lay down a measuring line from O so every spot on the track has a number: twenty meters, forty meters, sixty meters, and so on. <<UNFOCUS>> But is a number enough? If I say the runner is at sixty meters, have I really told you where she is? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Not quite, because sixty meters could be to the left or to the right. So we also <<FOCUS:direction-arrow>> fix a direction with this arrow, pointing forward along the track. <<WRITE_KEY:Position = reference point + distance + direction|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So a position is three things together: a fixed reference point, a distance from it, and a direction. <<PAUSE:short>> Watch the runner. At one instant she is here, <<FOCUS:position-b+b-label>> at point B, twenty meters from O along the track. A few seconds later she is here, <<FOCUS:position-a+a-label>> at point A, sixty meters from O. <<UNFOCUS>> Her position, measured from our flag, has changed. <<WRITE_TEXT:position changes in time means motion|id=text-1>> And that is exactly what motion is: when an object's position relative to the reference point changes as time passes, we say it is moving. <<PAUSE:short>> Flip it around: if her position from O never changed, instant after instant, she would be standing still, at rest. <<PAUSE:short>> So next time someone says something is twenty meters away, ask them the two questions that turn a useless number into a real location: from where, and which way?

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_3:track_journey>> If you walk all the way around a running track and end up exactly where you started, your average speed is big, but your average velocity is zero. How can both be true at once? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Speed versus velocity|id=sec-1>> You already know average speed. It just tells us how fast something moves, and we get it by dividing the total distance travelled by the time taken. Here is the key: <<FOCUS:path-curve>> distance is just a length, a plain number with no direction at all. <<UNFOCUS>> So average speed, built only from distance, is also just a number with no direction. <<PAUSE:short>> Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the time taken. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{average speed} = \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{time}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now look at <<TRACE:displacement-arrow>> this short straight arrow from where you started to where you finished. That straight-line shortcut, with its direction, is the displacement. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:velocity = displacement over time|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Average velocity is displacement divided by time. Because displacement carries a direction, average velocity carries a direction too. <<PAUSE:short>> Average velocity is the displacement divided by the time taken, and it points in the direction of the displacement. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{average velocity} = \dfrac{\text{displacement}}{\text{time}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> So back to our puzzle. You ran <<FOCUS:path-curve>> the whole long way around, building up a real total distance, so your average speed was clearly large. <<UNFOCUS>> But what happens to the displacement when you finish exactly where you began? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Back to start means zero displacement, so zero average velocity|id=key-1>> The start and the end <<FOCUS:start-point+end-point>> are the same spot, so the straight-line displacement shrinks to nothing. <<UNFOCUS>> Zero displacement means zero average velocity, even though you sprinted the whole way. <<PAUSE:short>> That is the whole idea. <<FOCUS:path-curve>> The winding distance feeds the speed; <<FOCUS:displacement-arrow>> the straight arrow feeds the velocity. <<UNFOCUS>> Same journey, two very different answers. And one last thing about steadiness. If something travels equal distances in every equal slice of time, that is uniform motion and the speed stays constant. Unequal distances mean it is speeding up or slowing down.

segments.narration_chapter: Why does your body lurch forward the instant a bus slams its brakes, even though nothing actually pushed you? <<PAUSE:long>> That jolt you feel is your body sensing something change very fast: its velocity. One moment you were moving, the next you nearly weren't. <<PAUSE:short>> The physics word for how quickly velocity changes is acceleration. The bigger the jolt, the more violent the acceleration. <<SECTION:Average acceleration|id=sec-1>> So here is the heart of it: average acceleration is just how much the velocity changed, divided by how long it took to change. <<PAUSE:short>> Change in velocity means the velocity you ended with minus the velocity you started with. If you started at rest and ended fast, that change is large. <<WRITE_TEXT:change in velocity over time taken|id=text-1>> Now squeeze that big change into a tiny time, and you get a huge acceleration. Squeeze it into a long time, and the acceleration is gentle. <<WRITE_KEY:a equals change in velocity divided by time|id=key-1>> In plain words: take the final velocity, subtract the initial velocity, then divide by the time interval. That single number is the average acceleration. <<PAUSE:short>> Average acceleration is the final velocity minus the initial velocity, all divided by the time taken for that change. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a = \dfrac{v - u}{t_2 - t_1}|id=eq-1|boxed>> And because we divide a velocity, in meters per second, by a time in seconds, the unit comes out as meters per second squared. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_4:accel_direction_pair>> <<SECTION:Acceleration has direction|id=sec-2>> But here is the part people forget: acceleration is not just a number, it has a direction, just like velocity. When you are speeding up, the acceleration <<FOCUS:velocity-speeding+accel-speeding>> points the same way you are moving. <<UNFOCUS>> Velocity and acceleration march together. <<PAUSE:short>> So when does the acceleration <<FOCUS:velocity-slowing+accel-slowing>> point backwards, against your motion? <<UNFOCUS>> Think about that braking bus. <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. A bus is moving on a long straight highway. First, the driver presses the accelerator for ten seconds, and the velocity rises from thirty-six kilometers per hour, which is ten meters per second, up to fifty-four kilometers per hour, which is fifteen meters per second. Then later, the driver presses the brakes and the bus comes to a stop in five seconds. We want the average acceleration in both intervals. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the average acceleration when the accelerator is pressed, and when the brakes are pressed.|id=ex-q-1>> Let's handle part one, when the accelerator is pressed. Here the initial velocity u is ten meters per second, the final velocity v is fifteen meters per second, and the time t is ten seconds. Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by time. <<WRITE_STEP:Part (i): u = 10 m/s, v = 15 m/s, t = 10 s|id=ex-step-1>> So a equals fifteen meters per second minus ten meters per second, all divided by ten seconds. That gives five meters per second over ten seconds, which is zero point five meters per second squared. Since the magnitude of the velocity is increasing, this acceleration acts <<FOCUS:velocity-speeding+accel-speeding>> in the direction of the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (15 - 10) / 10 = 5 / 10 = 0.5 m/s^2, along velocity|id=ex-step-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now part two, when the brakes are pressed. Here the initial velocity u is fifty-four kilometers per hour, which is fifteen meters per second, the final velocity v is zero meters per second, and the time t is five seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:Part (ii): u = 15 m/s, v = 0 m/s, t = 5 s|id=ex-step-3>> So a equals zero meters per second minus fifteen meters per second, all over five seconds. That's negative fifteen meters per second divided by five seconds, which is negative three meters per second squared. The minus sign tells us the acceleration <<FOCUS:velocity-slowing+accel-slowing>> acts opposite to the direction of velocity, because the bus is slowing down. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (0 - 15) / 5 = -15 / 5 = -3 m/s^2, opposite to velocity|id=ex-step-4>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the two answers are: zero point five meters per second squared in the direction of velocity when accelerating, and negative three meters per second squared, opposite to velocity, when braking. <<WRITE_ANSWER:(i) a = 0.5 m/s^2 (along velocity); (ii) a = -3 m/s^2 (opposite velocity)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. An object is dropped from a height and falls straight down along a vertical path. As it comes down, its velocity keeps increasing: at one second the velocity is nine point eight meters per second, at two seconds it's nineteen point six meters per second, at three seconds it's twenty-nine point four meters per second, and at four seconds it's thirty-nine point two meters per second. We want to find the magnitude of the average acceleration in every successive one-second interval. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A falling object has velocity 9.8, 19.6, 29.4, 39.2 m/s at t = 1, 2, 3, 4 s. Find the average acceleration in each interval.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the first interval, between zero seconds and one second. Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the change in time. So that's nine point eight minus zero meters per second, over one minus zero seconds, which gives nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 0 to 1 s: a = (9.8 - 0)/(1 - 0) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now the interval between one second and two seconds. The velocity goes from nine point eight to nineteen point six meters per second. So we take nineteen point six minus nine point eight, over two minus one seconds, and again we get nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 1 to 2 s: a = (19.6 - 9.8)/(2 - 1) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Continuing for the next two intervals: between two and three seconds, twenty-nine point four minus nineteen point six over one second is again nine point eight meters per second squared; and between three and four seconds, thirty-nine point two minus twenty-nine point four over one second is once more nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 2 to 3 s: a = (29.4 - 19.6)/(3 - 2) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 3 to 4 s: a = (39.2 - 29.4)/(4 - 3) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-4>> Notice that each one-second interval gives the same average acceleration of nine point eight meters per second squared, so the average acceleration is constant. And since the velocity is increasing in the direction of motion, the acceleration is in the direction of motion as well. This is the acceleration due to gravity, denoted by g, equal to nine point eight meters per second squared, directed downward in the direction of motion. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Average acceleration = 9.8 m/s^2, constant, in the direction of motion (g, due to gravity)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> When you slow down, the acceleration <<FOCUS:velocity-slowing+accel-slowing>> points opposite to your velocity, dragging your speed down. <<UNFOCUS>> That backwards-pointing acceleration is exactly what threw you forward in your seat. <<PAUSE:short>> So next time you feel that jolt, you will know: your body just measured an acceleration, and even felt which way it pointed.

One moment you were moving, the next you nearly weren't. <<PAUSE:short>> The physics word for how quickly velocity changes is acceleration. The bigger the jolt, the more violent the acceleration. <<SECTION:Average acceleration|id=sec-1>>So here is the heart of it: average acceleration is just how much the velocity changed, divided by how long it took to change. <<PAUSE:short>> Change in velocity means the velocity you ended with minus the velocity you started with. If you started at rest and ended fast, that change is large. <<WRITE_TEXT:change in velocity over time taken|id=text-1>>Now squeeze that big change into a tiny time, and you get a huge acceleration. Squeeze it into a long time, and the acceleration is gentle. <<WRITE_KEY:a equals change in velocity divided by time|id=key-1>>In plain words: take the final velocity, subtract the initial velocity, then divide by the time interval. That single number is the average acceleration. <<PAUSE:short>> Average acceleration is the final velocity minus the initial velocity, all divided by the time taken for that change. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a = \dfrac{v - u}{t_2 - t_1}|id=eq-1|boxed>> And because we divide a velocity, in meters per second, by a time in seconds, the unit comes out as meters per second squared. <<FOCUS:velocity-speeding>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_4:accel_direction_pair>> <<SECTION:Acceleration has direction|id=sec-2>>But here is the part people forget: acceleration is not just a number, it has a direction, just like velocity. When you are speeding up, the acceleration points the same way you are moving. Velocity and acceleration march together. <<POINT:accel-speeding>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:velocity-slowing>> So when does the acceleration point backwards, against your motion? Think about that braking bus. <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. A bus is moving on a long straight highway. First, the driver presses the accelerator for ten seconds, and the velocity rises from thirty-six kilometers per hour, which is ten meters per second, up to fifty-four kilometers per hour, which is fifteen meters per second. Then later, the driver presses the brakes and the bus comes to a stop in five seconds. We want the average acceleration in both intervals. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the average acceleration when the accelerator is pressed, and when the brakes are pressed.|id=ex-q-1>> Let's handle part one, when the accelerator is pressed. Here the initial velocity u is ten meters per second, the final velocity v is fifteen meters per second, and the time t is ten seconds. Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by time. <<WRITE_STEP:Part (i): u = 10 m/s, v = 15 m/s, t = 10 s|id=ex-step-1>> So a equals fifteen meters per second minus ten meters per second, all divided by ten seconds. That gives five meters per second over ten seconds, which is zero point five meters per second squared. Since the magnitude of the velocity is increasing, this acceleration acts in the direction of the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (15 - 10) / 10 = 5 / 10 = 0.5 m/s^2, along velocity|id=ex-step-2>> Now part two, when the brakes are pressed. Here the initial velocity u is fifty-four kilometers per hour, which is fifteen meters per second, the final velocity v is zero meters per second, and the time t is five seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:Part (ii): u = 15 m/s, v = 0 m/s, t = 5 s|id=ex-step-3>> So a equals zero meters per second minus fifteen meters per second, all over five seconds. That's negative fifteen meters per second divided by five seconds, which is negative three meters per second squared. The minus sign tells us the acceleration acts opposite to the direction of velocity, because the bus is slowing down. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (0 - 15) / 5 = -15 / 5 = -3 m/s^2, opposite to velocity|id=ex-step-4>> So the two answers are: zero point five meters per second squared in the direction of velocity when accelerating, and negative three meters per second squared, opposite to velocity, when braking. <<WRITE_ANSWER:(i) a = 0.5 m/s^2 (along velocity); (ii) a = -3 m/s^2 (opposite velocity)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. An object is dropped from a height and falls straight down along a vertical path. As it comes down, its velocity keeps increasing: at one second the velocity is nine point eight meters per second, at two seconds it's nineteen point six meters per second, at three seconds it's twenty-nine point four meters per second, and at four seconds it's thirty-nine point two meters per second. We want to find the magnitude of the average acceleration in every successive one-second interval. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A falling object has velocity 9.8, 19.6, 29.4, 39.2 m/s at t = 1, 2, 3, 4 s. Find the average acceleration in each interval.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the first interval, between zero seconds and one second. Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the change in time. So that's nine point eight minus zero meters per second, over one minus zero seconds, which gives nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 0 to 1 s: a = (9.8 - 0)/(1 - 0) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now the interval between one second and two seconds. The velocity goes from nine point eight to nineteen point six meters per second. So we take nineteen point six minus nine point eight, over two minus one seconds, and again we get nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 1 to 2 s: a = (19.6 - 9.8)/(2 - 1) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Continuing for the next two intervals: between two and three seconds, twenty-nine point four minus nineteen point six over one second is again nine point eight meters per second squared; and between three and four seconds, thirty-nine point two minus twenty-nine point four over one second is once more nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 2 to 3 s: a = (29.4 - 19.6)/(3 - 2) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-3>><<WRITE_STEP:Interval 3 to 4 s: a = (39.2 - 29.4)/(4 - 3) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-4>> Notice that each one-second interval gives the same average acceleration of nine point eight meters per second squared, so the average acceleration is constant. And since the velocity is increasing in the direction of motion, the acceleration is in the direction of motion as well. This is the acceleration due to gravity, denoted by g, equal to nine point eight meters per second squared, directed downward in the direction of motion. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Average acceleration = 9.8 m/s^2, constant, in the direction of motion (g, due to gravity)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> When you slow down, the acceleration points opposite to your velocity, dragging your speed down. That backwards-pointing acceleration is exactly what threw you forward in your seat. <<POINT:accel-slowing>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So next time you feel that jolt, you will know: your body just measured an acceleration, and even felt which way it pointed.

segments.narration_chapter: Two cars race away from a traffic light. Without a single calculation, can you say which one speeds up faster? You can — if you let them draw you a picture. <<PAUSE:long>> Up to now we've described motion with words and numbers: it moved ten meters, it took two seconds. True, but flat. <<SECTION:Why graph motion?|id=sec-1>> A graph gives us something better — a picture of the whole journey we can take in at a glance. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_2:position_time_graph>> Here's the trick. We pick two things that are connected — say, position and time — and we draw how one changes as the other changes. <<FOCUS:time-axis>> Time runs along the bottom, <<FOCUS:position-axis>> position climbs up the side. <<UNFOCUS>> Every dot on this picture answers one question: where was the object at this moment? Watch what happens when the object moves at a steady pace. The dots line up <<TRACE:steady-line>> into a straight, rising line. <<WRITE_TEXT:Steady motion = straight rising line|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And right there is the payoff: the whole story of the motion has become one picture you can read in a heartbeat — no calculation needed. <<PAUSE:short>> Now look closely at the line. Notice <<FOCUS:steady-line>> how steeply it climbs as we move to the right. <<UNFOCUS>> That steepness has a meaning. In the same slice of time, <<FOCUS:slope-marker>> a steeper line covers more position — and covering more distance in the same time is exactly what we mean by going faster. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So let's race the cars. <<TRACE:steep-line>> Here's a second line, climbing more steeply than the first. <<FOCUS:steep-line+steady-line>> Steeper line, faster car. <<UNFOCUS>> You read the answer straight off the picture — that's the power we were after. <<WRITE_KEY:Steeper line means moving faster|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> What about an object that's just sitting still — what would its line look like? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. An object is dropped from a height, and we track its velocity each second as it falls. At time zero seconds, its initial velocity is zero meters per second. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: An object dropped from a height — find how its velocity changes each second.|id=ex-q-1>> Now let's read off the velocity at each second. At one second the velocity is nine point eight meters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 0 s, v = 0 m/s|id=ex-step-1-1>> At two seconds it is nineteen point six meters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 1 s, v = 9.8 m/s|id=ex-step-1-2>> At three seconds it is twenty-nine point four meters per second, and at four seconds it is thirty-nine point two meters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 2 s, v = 19.6 m/s|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 3 s, v = 29.4 m/s|id=ex-step-1-4>> <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 4 s, v = 39.2 m/s|id=ex-step-1-5>> Notice that every second the velocity goes up by the same nine point eight meters per second. That equal jump each second means the acceleration is constant. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Velocity increases by 9.8 m/s every second → acceleration is constant|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Time keeps marching on, but position never changes — so <<FOCUS:flat-segment>> the line goes flat. <<UNFOCUS>> A horizontal line means standing still. The shape itself tells you the story. And that's the whole idea. <<WRITE_TEXT:Slope of position-time graph = speed|id=text-2>> A line that rises is moving, a steeper rise is faster, a flat line is at rest — the picture is the motion, made visible. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: Here's a table: at one second the car is at twenty meters, at two seconds forty meters, at three seconds sixty meters. Quick, without doing any maths, is it speeding up or slowing down? Hard to tell from a row of numbers, isn't it? <<PAUSE:long>> That's the whole problem with a table. The numbers are correct, but your eye can't see the story inside them. So let's turn that table into something you can read in one glance. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_2_1:position_time_axes>> <<SECTION:Building the axes|id=sec-1>> We start by drawing <<FOCUS:x-axis+y-axis>> two lines that cross at right angles. The corner where they meet has a name, <<FOCUS:origin>> the origin. The horizontal line is <<FOCUS:x-axis>> the X-axis, and along it we'll put time. The vertical line is <<FOCUS:y-axis>> the Y-axis, and up it we'll put position. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Time on X-axis, position on Y-axis|id=text-1>> Notice <<FOCUS:grid>> the faint squares, that's graph paper. <<UNFOCUS>> Each square is a fixed amount, so every point lands in exactly the right spot. Now, how does one row of the table become one dot on this grid? Take the row for two seconds and forty meters. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Go across to the time, then up to the position|id=step-1>> You go <<TRACE:trace-across>> across the X-axis until you reach two seconds, then you <<TRACE:trace-up>> travel straight up until you reach forty meters. Where those two meet, <<FOCUS:point-2s>> you put a dot. <<WRITE_KEY:Each table row becomes one point: across to the time, up to the position|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That single dot now carries both facts at once, the time and the position, locked into one spot on the picture. <<PAUSE:short>> Do that for every row of the table, and you get <<FOCUS:all-points>> a whole scatter of dots marching across the page. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And now look, the answer to my opening question is staring right at you. The dots climb in <<TRACE:all-points>> a perfectly straight, even line. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have data for a vehicle moving on a straight road. At zero seconds, the position is zero meters; at one second, twenty meters; at two seconds, forty meters; at three seconds, sixty meters; at four seconds, eighty meters; at five seconds, one hundred meters; and at six seconds, one hundred twenty meters. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Plot the position-time graph for a vehicle: (0s, 0m), (1s, 20m), (2s, 40m), (3s, 60m), (4s, 80m), (5s, 100m), (6s, 120m)|id=ex-q-1>> First, we set up the axes. We show time along the X-axis and position along the Y-axis. For the scale, on the X-axis five divisions equal one second, and on the Y-axis five divisions equal twenty meters. <<WRITE_STEP:Axes: time on X-axis, position on Y-axis|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Scale: X-axis 5 divisions = 1 s; Y-axis 5 divisions = 20 m|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we plot the first point. At zero seconds the position is also zero meters, so this point is the origin itself. <<WRITE_STEP:At 0 s, position 0 m → plot at the origin|id=ex-step-1-3>> Next, at one second the vehicle is at twenty meters. We find the point representing one second on the X-axis and draw a line parallel to the Y-axis. Then from twenty meters on the Y-axis we draw a line parallel to the X-axis. Where these two lines intersect is the position twenty meters at time one second. <<WRITE_STEP:At 1 s, draw line parallel to Y-axis; from 20 m, line parallel to X-axis; intersection = point (1 s, 20 m)|id=ex-step-1-4>> We plot all the remaining points the same way: forty meters at two seconds, sixty meters at three seconds, eighty meters at four seconds, one hundred meters at five seconds, and one hundred twenty meters at six seconds. Then we connect all the points. <<WRITE_STEP:Similarly plot (2s,40m), (3s,60m), (4s,80m), (5s,100m), (6s,120m); connect all points|id=ex-step-1-5>> And the answer is that the plotted points form a straight line. For this data, the position-time graph is a straight line, which tells us the motion is at constant speed. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The position-time graph is a straight line (constant-speed motion)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A vehicle starts from rest and speeds up, and we're given its position at different times. At zero seconds, the position is zero meters; at two seconds, one meter; at four seconds, four meters; at six seconds, nine meters; at eight seconds, sixteen meters; at ten seconds, twenty-five meters; and at twelve seconds, thirty-six meters. We need to plot the position-time graph for this. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Plot position-time graph for a vehicle starting from rest and speeding up|id=ex-q-1>> We start by choosing a sensible scale so the points fit nicely on the page. On the X-axis, we let five divisions equal two seconds, and on the Y-axis, we let five divisions equal five meters. <<WRITE_STEP:X-axis: 5 divisions = 2 seconds|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Y-axis: 5 divisions = 5 meters|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we mark each pair of values. Time on the horizontal axis, position on the vertical axis. So we plot zero seconds at zero meters, two seconds at one meter, four seconds at four meters, and six seconds at nine meters. <<WRITE_STEP:Plot (0,0), (2,1), (4,4), (6,9)|id=ex-step-1-3>> Then we continue marking the remaining points: eight seconds at sixteen meters, ten seconds at twenty-five meters, and twelve seconds at thirty-six meters. <<WRITE_STEP:Plot (8,16), (10,25), (12,36)|id=ex-step-1-4>> Now look closely at the marked points. Unlike the case of uniform motion, these points do not fall on a straight line. Because the vehicle is speeding up, the position grows faster and faster, so when we join the points we get a curve. <<WRITE_STEP:Points do NOT lie on a straight line|id=ex-step-1-5>> And the answer is: the position-time graph is a curve, not a straight line, showing that the vehicle is speeding up. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The points form a curve, not a straight line|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> A straight, evenly rising line means equal distance in equal time, the car is moving steadily, not speeding up and not slowing down. The picture told you in one second what the table hid. So remember the recipe: time across the bottom, position up the side, and every row of the table becomes one point you read by going across then up. That's how numbers become a picture you can actually understand. <<PAUSE:short>>
