lesson_plans.title: Motion in a Straight Line

hook.text: A ball dropped from your hand, a train on a track, a swimmer racing across a pool — what do all three secretly have in common?

crucial_facts: Motion along a single straight path — forward or backward only, no curves or turns — is called linear motion, and it is the simplest kind of motion.
To describe any motion, you must first be able to state the object's position at each instant of time.

diagrams.purpose: Show an object confined to a single straight line, moving only forward or backward, to make 'linear motion' visually concrete.

required_elements.description: A long horizontal straight line representing the single path the object is confined to.
A small ball or car sitting on the line that can slide forward and backward along it.
An arrow pointing right along the line indicating forward motion.
An arrow pointing left along the line indicating backward motion.
A marked dot on the line showing the object's position at one instant of time.

choreography.narration: A ball dropped from your hand, a train on a track, a swimmer racing across a pool — what do all three secretly have in common?
Every single one of them moves along a straight path — no curving, no swerving, just a clean line from here to there.
<<SECTION:Motion in a Straight Line|id=sec-1>>Let me put one object on that line, and notice it can only do two things.
It can move forward, this way along the line.
Or it can move backward, the other way. That's it — there is no third option, because it's stuck on one single line.

<<WRITE_KEY:Linear motion = motion along one straight line, forward or backward only|id=key-1>>This is what we call linear motion, or motion in a straight line — and because there are no turns to worry about, it is the simplest kind of motion there is.
And that simplicity is exactly why we begin here — master the straight line, and curves and turns become just straight lines stitched together later.
Now here's a fair question: if the object is just sliding along this line, how would I actually describe where it is at any moment?
<<WRITE_TEXT:Position = where the object is on the line|id=text-1>>I drop a marker right where it sits — that single dot on the line tells me its position at this instant of time.

<<WRITE_KEY:To describe motion, first describe position at each instant of time|id=key-2>>So before we can talk about how fast or how far, we must first be able to state the object's position at each instant of time.
That one idea — pinning down position instant by instant — is the foundation everything else about motion is built on.
So remember the two takeaways: straight-line motion is the simplest motion, forward or backward only — and to describe it, you start by describing position. Next, we'll do exactly that.

lesson_plans.title: Describing Position: From Where, and Which Way?

hook.text: If I tell you a treasure is buried twenty meters away, could you find it? Twenty meters from what? And in which direction? You'd be digging forever.

crucial_facts: A position needs three things: a fixed reference point, a distance from it, and a direction.
An object is moving if its position relative to the reference point changes with time; otherwise it is at rest.

diagrams.purpose: Show that position only becomes meaningful once we fix an origin and read off distance plus direction along a marked straight line.

required_elements.description: A clearly labelled point O at the left end of a horizontal straight track, marked as zero meters.
A horizontal straight line with distance ticks marked at twenty, forty, sixty, eighty and one hundred meters running rightward from O.
A dot labelled B sitting at the twenty meter mark, an earlier position of the runner.
A dot labelled A sitting at the sixty meter mark, a later position of the runner.
An arrow pointing rightward from O along the track indicating the chosen positive direction.

choreography.narration: If I tell you a treasure is buried twenty meters away, could you find it? Twenty meters from what? And in which direction? You'd be digging forever.

<<SECTION:Describing Position|id=sec-1>>The problem is that distance alone floats in empty space. To pin anything down, we first plant a flag: a single fixed point that everyone agrees to measure from.
We call that flag the reference point, and here it sits at O, the starting line of a running track, which we call zero meters.
Now we lay down a measuring line from O so every spot on the track has a number: twenty meters, forty meters, sixty meters, and so on.
But is a number enough? If I say the runner is at sixty meters, have I really told you where she is?
Not quite, because sixty meters could be to the left or to the right. So we also fix a direction with this arrow, pointing forward along the track.
<<WRITE_KEY:Position = reference point + distance + direction|id=key-1>>So a position is three things together: a fixed reference point, a distance from it, and a direction.
Watch the runner. At one instant she is here, at point B, twenty meters from O along the track.
A few seconds later she is here, at point A, sixty meters from O. Her position, measured from our flag, has changed.

<<WRITE_TEXT:position changes in time means motion|id=text-1>>And that is exactly what motion is: when an object's position relative to the reference point changes as time passes, we say it is moving.
Flip it around: if her position from O never changed, instant after instant, she would be standing still, at rest.
So next time someone says something is twenty meters away, ask them the two questions that turn a useless number into a real location: from where, and which way?

lesson_plans.title: Distance Travelled and Displacement

hook.text: An athlete runs one hundred sixty meters around a track and ends up only forty meters from where she started. So how far did she travel — one hundred sixty, or forty?

crucial_facts: Distance travelled is the total ground covered along the path; displacement is the straight-line change in position from start to finish, and it has a direction.
Distance is a single number, but displacement always needs both a size and a direction.

diagrams.purpose: Show the straight track with start point O and positions B and A, so distance-along-path can be visually distinguished from start-to-end displacement.

required_elements.description: The starting point O at the zero-meter mark on the straight track.
Point B at the forty-meter mark on the track, where the athlete finishes.
Point A at the one-hundred-meter mark, the furthest point reached.
The straight horizontal track marked in meters from zero upward.
The forward path from O to A traced along the track.
The return path from A back to B traced along the track.
A straight arrow from O to B representing the net displacement, pointing forward.

choreography.narration: An athlete runs one hundred sixty meters around a track and ends up only forty meters from where she started. So how far did she travel — one hundred sixty, or forty?
Here's the track. She starts at this point, which we'll call O, at the zero-meter mark.
<<SECTION:Distance travelled|id=sec-1>>She runs forward, past point B, all the way to point A at the one-hundred-meter mark. Watch her feet cover that ground.
Then she turns around and runs back from A to B, covering another sixty meters of ground.

<<WRITE_EQUATION:160 = 100 + 60|id=eq-dist>>Add up every bit of path her feet touched: one hundred plus sixty is one hundred sixty meters. That total ground covered is the distance travelled, and it doesn't care which direction she went.
Now I'm going to ask a completely different question. Forget the path. Where did she start, and where did she actually end up?
She started at O and finished at B. So the only thing that matters now is this straight gap between start and finish.
<<SECTION:Displacement|id=sec-2>>That straight-line change in position is forty meters, pointing forward. We call it the displacement.

<<WRITE_KEY:Distance = total path covered. Displacement = straight-line change in position, with direction.|id=key-1>>So distance travelled is the total ground covered along the path, but displacement is the straight-line change in position from start to finish — and displacement has a direction.
And here's the catch that trips everyone up: distance is just a single number, but displacement always needs two things — a size and a direction.

<<WRITE_TEXT:If she'd returned all the way to O, displacement = 0|id=text-1>>Imagine she'd run all the way back to O. The distance travelled would be even bigger, but the displacement would be zero — she'd be exactly where she began.
So next time someone says how far did you go, ask them which they mean — the ground you covered, or how far you ended up from the start. They're rarely the same number.

lesson_plans.title: Average Speed and Average Velocity

hook.text: If you walk all the way around a running track and end up exactly where you started, your average speed is big — but your average velocity is zero. How can both be true at once?

crucial_facts: Average speed uses the total distance travelled, so it is just a number; average velocity uses displacement, so it has a direction.
If a journey returns you to where you started, the displacement is zero, so the average velocity is zero no matter how fast you moved.

diagrams.purpose: Show a curved path from start to end so the long winding distance and the short straight-line displacement can be compared side by side.

required_elements.description: A marked starting position labelled Start on the left.
A marked finishing position labelled End, some distance to the right of start.
A long winding curved path looping from start-point to end-point, representing the actual distance travelled.
A straight arrow from start-point directly to end-point, representing displacement with its direction.

choreography.narration: If you walk all the way around a running track and end up exactly where you started, your average speed is big, but your average velocity is zero. How can both be true at once?
<<SECTION:Speed versus velocity|id=sec-1>>You already know average speed. It just tells us how fast something moves, and we get it by dividing the total distance travelled by the time taken.
Here is the key: distance is just a length, a plain number with no direction at all. So average speed, built only from distance, is also just a number with no direction.
Now look at this short straight arrow from where you started to where you finished. That straight-line shortcut, with its direction, is the displacement.
<<WRITE_TEXT:velocity = displacement over time|id=text-1>>Average velocity is displacement divided by time. Because displacement carries a direction, average velocity carries a direction too.
So back to our puzzle. You ran the whole long way around, building up a real total distance, so your average speed was clearly large.
But what happens to the displacement when you finish exactly where you began?

<<WRITE_KEY:Back to start means zero displacement, so zero average velocity|id=key-1>>The start and the end are the same spot, so the straight-line displacement shrinks to nothing. Zero displacement means zero average velocity, even though you sprinted the whole way.
That is the whole idea. The winding distance feeds the speed; the straight arrow feeds the velocity. Same journey, two very different answers.

And one last thing about steadiness. If something travels equal distances in every equal slice of time, that is uniform motion and the speed stays constant. Unequal distances mean it is speeding up or slowing down.

equations.explanation_in_words: Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the time taken.
Average velocity is the displacement divided by the time taken, and it points in the direction of the displacement.

lesson_plans.title: Average Acceleration: The Physics of the Jolt

hook.text: Why does your body lurch forward the instant a bus slams its brakes — even though nothing pushed you?

crucial_facts: Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time interval — final velocity minus initial velocity, over time.
Acceleration has direction: it points the same way as velocity when you speed up, and opposite to velocity when you slow down.

diagrams.purpose: Show that acceleration points along velocity when speeding up and against velocity when slowing down, using two side-by-side arrow pairs.

required_elements.description: A rightward velocity arrow for an object that is speeding up.
A rightward acceleration arrow, same direction as velocity-speeding, drawn below it.
A rightward velocity arrow for an object that is slowing down.
A leftward acceleration arrow, opposite to velocity-slowing, drawn below it.

choreography.narration: Why does your body lurch forward the instant a bus slams its brakes, even though nothing actually pushed you?
That jolt you feel is your body sensing something change very fast: its velocity. One moment you were moving, the next you nearly weren't.
The physics word for how quickly velocity changes is acceleration. The bigger the jolt, the more violent the acceleration.
<<SECTION:Average acceleration|id=sec-1>>So here is the heart of it: average acceleration is just how much the velocity changed, divided by how long it took to change.
Change in velocity means the velocity you ended with minus the velocity you started with. If you started at rest and ended fast, that change is large.
<<WRITE_TEXT:change in velocity over time taken|id=text-1>>Now squeeze that big change into a tiny time, and you get a huge acceleration. Squeeze it into a long time, and the acceleration is gentle.

<<WRITE_KEY:a equals change in velocity divided by time|id=key-1>>In plain words: take the final velocity, subtract the initial velocity, then divide by the time interval. That single number is the average acceleration.
And because we divide a velocity, in meters per second, by a time in seconds, the unit comes out as meters per second squared.
<<SECTION:Acceleration has direction|id=sec-2>>But here is the part people forget: acceleration is not just a number, it has a direction, just like velocity.
When you are speeding up, the acceleration points the same way you are moving. Velocity and acceleration march together.
So when does the acceleration point backwards, against your motion? Think about that braking bus.

Here's an example from the chapter. A bus is moving on a long straight highway. First, the driver presses the accelerator for ten seconds, and the velocity rises from thirty-six kilometers per hour, which is ten meters per second, up to fifty-four kilometers per hour, which is fifteen meters per second. Then later, the driver presses the brakes and the bus comes to a stop in five seconds. We want the average acceleration in both intervals. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the average acceleration when the accelerator is pressed, and when the brakes are pressed.|id=ex-q-1>>

Let's handle part one, when the accelerator is pressed. Here the initial velocity u is ten meters per second, the final velocity v is fifteen meters per second, and the time t is ten seconds. Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by time. <<WRITE_STEP:Part (i): u = 10 m/s, v = 15 m/s, t = 10 s|id=ex-step-1>>

So a equals fifteen meters per second minus ten meters per second, all divided by ten seconds. That gives five meters per second over ten seconds, which is zero point five meters per second squared. Since the magnitude of the velocity is increasing, this acceleration acts in the direction of the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (15 - 10) / 10 = 5 / 10 = 0.5 m/s^2, along velocity|id=ex-step-2>>

Now part two, when the brakes are pressed. Here the initial velocity u is fifty-four kilometers per hour, which is fifteen meters per second, the final velocity v is zero meters per second, and the time t is five seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:Part (ii): u = 15 m/s, v = 0 m/s, t = 5 s|id=ex-step-3>>

So a equals zero meters per second minus fifteen meters per second, all over five seconds. That's negative fifteen meters per second divided by five seconds, which is negative three meters per second squared. The minus sign tells us the acceleration acts opposite to the direction of velocity, because the bus is slowing down. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (0 - 15) / 5 = -15 / 5 = -3 m/s^2, opposite to velocity|id=ex-step-4>>

So the two answers are: zero point five meters per second squared in the direction of velocity when accelerating, and negative three meters per second squared, opposite to velocity, when braking. <<WRITE_ANSWER:(i) a = 0.5 m/s^2 (along velocity); (ii) a = -3 m/s^2 (opposite velocity)|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. An object is dropped from a height and falls straight down along a vertical path. As it comes down, its velocity keeps increasing: at one second the velocity is nine point eight meters per second, at two seconds it's nineteen point six meters per second, at three seconds it's twenty-nine point four meters per second, and at four seconds it's thirty-nine point two meters per second. We want to find the magnitude of the average acceleration in every successive one-second interval. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A falling object has velocity 9.8, 19.6, 29.4, 39.2 m/s at t = 1, 2, 3, 4 s. Find the average acceleration in each interval.|id=ex-q-1>>

We start with the first interval, between zero seconds and one second. Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the change in time. So that's nine point eight minus zero meters per second, over one minus zero seconds, which gives nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 0 to 1 s: a = (9.8 - 0)/(1 - 0) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Now the interval between one second and two seconds. The velocity goes from nine point eight to nineteen point six meters per second. So we take nineteen point six minus nine point eight, over two minus one seconds, and again we get nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 1 to 2 s: a = (19.6 - 9.8)/(2 - 1) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Continuing for the next two intervals: between two and three seconds, twenty-nine point four minus nineteen point six over one second is again nine point eight meters per second squared; and between three and four seconds, thirty-nine point two minus twenty-nine point four over one second is once more nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 2 to 3 s: a = (29.4 - 19.6)/(3 - 2) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-3>><<WRITE_STEP:Interval 3 to 4 s: a = (39.2 - 29.4)/(4 - 3) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-4>>

Notice that each one-second interval gives the same average acceleration of nine point eight meters per second squared, so the average acceleration is constant. And since the velocity is increasing in the direction of motion, the acceleration is in the direction of motion as well. This is the acceleration due to gravity, denoted by g, equal to nine point eight meters per second squared, directed downward in the direction of motion. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Average acceleration = 9.8 m/s^2, constant, in the direction of motion (g, due to gravity)|id=ex-ans-1>>
When you slow down, the acceleration points opposite to your velocity, dragging your speed down. That backwards-pointing acceleration is exactly what threw you forward in your seat.
So next time you feel that jolt, you will know: your body just measured an acceleration, and even felt which way it pointed.

equations.explanation_in_words: Average acceleration is the final velocity minus the initial velocity, all divided by the time taken for that change.

lesson_plans.title: Graphical Representation of Motion

hook.text: Two cars race away from a traffic light. Without doing a single calculation, can you tell which one speeds up faster? You can — if you let them draw you a picture.

crucial_facts: A motion graph turns the story of how an object moves into a single picture you can read at a glance.
The steepness of the line — how fast the line climbs — tells you how fast the quantity is changing.

diagrams.purpose: Show how plotting position against time turns a moving object into a readable line whose steepness means speed.

required_elements.description: Horizontal axis labelled time in seconds, running left to right.
Vertical axis labelled position in meters, running bottom to top.
A straight line rising steadily from the origin, representing an object moving at constant speed.
A second straight line from the origin rising more steeply, representing a faster object.
A horizontal segment where position does not change over time, representing an object at rest.
A small right-triangle drawn under the steady line showing rise over run, marking the slope as speed.

choreography.narration: Two cars race away from a traffic light. Without a single calculation, can you say which one speeds up faster? You can — if you let them draw you a picture.

Up to now we've described motion with words and numbers: it moved ten meters, it took two seconds. True, but flat. <<SECTION:Why graph motion?|id=sec-1>>A graph gives us something better — a picture of the whole journey we can take in at a glance.
Here's the trick. We pick two things that are connected — say, position and time — and we draw how one changes as the other changes.
Time runs along the bottom, position climbs up the side. Every dot on this picture answers one question: where was the object at this moment?
Watch what happens when the object moves at a steady pace. The dots line up into a straight, rising line. <<WRITE_TEXT:Steady motion = straight rising line|id=text-1>>
And right there is the payoff: the whole story of the motion has become one picture you can read in a heartbeat — no calculation needed.
Now look closely at the line. Notice how steeply it climbs as we move to the right.
That steepness has a meaning. In the same slice of time, a steeper line covers more position — and covering more distance in the same time is exactly what we mean by going faster.
So let's race the cars. Here's a second line, climbing more steeply than the first.
Steeper line, faster car. You read the answer straight off the picture — that's the power we were after. <<WRITE_KEY:Steeper line means moving faster|id=key-1>>
What about an object that's just sitting still — what would its line look like?

Here's an example from the chapter. An object is dropped from a height, and we track its velocity each second as it falls. At time zero seconds, its initial velocity is zero meters per second. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: An object dropped from a height — find how its velocity changes each second.|id=ex-q-1>>

Now let's read off the velocity at each second. At one second the velocity is nine point eight meters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 0 s, v = 0 m/s|id=ex-step-1-1>> At two seconds it is nineteen point six meters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 1 s, v = 9.8 m/s|id=ex-step-1-2>> At three seconds it is twenty-nine point four meters per second, and at four seconds it is thirty-nine point two meters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 2 s, v = 19.6 m/s|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 3 s, v = 29.4 m/s|id=ex-step-1-4>> <<WRITE_STEP:At t = 4 s, v = 39.2 m/s|id=ex-step-1-5>>

Notice that every second the velocity goes up by the same nine point eight meters per second. That equal jump each second means the acceleration is constant. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Velocity increases by 9.8 m/s every second → acceleration is constant|id=ex-ans-1>>
Time keeps marching on, but position never changes — so the line goes flat. A horizontal line means standing still. The shape itself tells you the story.

And that's the whole idea. <<WRITE_TEXT:Slope of position-time graph = speed|id=text-2>>A line that rises is moving, a steeper rise is faster, a flat line is at rest — the picture is the motion, made visible.

lesson_plans.title: Plotting a Graph: Turning Numbers into a Picture

hook.text: Here's a table: at one second the car is at twenty meters, at two seconds forty meters, at three seconds sixty meters. Quick — without doing any maths, is it speeding up or slowing down? Hard to tell from numbers, isn't it?

crucial_facts: A graph turns a table of numbers into a single picture you can read at a glance, with time on the horizontal X-axis and position on the vertical Y-axis.
Each pair of values from the table becomes one point: go across to the time, then up to the position, and mark where they meet.

diagrams.purpose: Show the student exactly how a table of time-position pairs becomes points on a coordinate grid, building from bare axes to plotted points.

required_elements.description: The point O where the two axes cross, bottom-left of the grid.
Horizontal axis labelled Time in seconds, with marks at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
Vertical axis labelled Position in meters, with marks at 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120.
Faint square grid covering the plotting area, like graph paper.
The plotted point for time two seconds, position forty meters.
A horizontal guide line from the time mark up toward the point, showing the across-then-up method.
A vertical guide line from the position mark across toward the point.
The full set of plotted points for every row in the table, lying along a straight rising line.

choreography.narration: Here's a table: at one second the car is at twenty meters, at two seconds forty meters, at three seconds sixty meters. Quick, without doing any maths, is it speeding up or slowing down? Hard to tell from a row of numbers, isn't it?
That's the whole problem with a table. The numbers are correct, but your eye can't see the story inside them. So let's turn that table into something you can read in one glance.
<<SECTION:Building the axes|id=sec-1>>We start by drawing two lines that cross at right angles. The corner where they meet has a name, the origin.
The horizontal line is the X-axis, and along it we'll put time. The vertical line is the Y-axis, and up it we'll put position.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Time on X-axis, position on Y-axis|id=text-1>>Notice the faint squares, that's graph paper. Each square is a fixed amount, so every point lands in exactly the right spot.
Now, how does one row of the table become one dot on this grid? Take the row for two seconds and forty meters.

<<WRITE_STEP:Go across to the time, then up to the position|id=step-1>>You go across the X-axis until you reach two seconds, then you travel straight up until you reach forty meters. Where those two meet, you put a dot.

<<WRITE_KEY:Each table row becomes one point: across to the time, up to the position|id=key-1>>That single dot now carries both facts at once, the time and the position, locked into one spot on the picture.
Do that for every row of the table, and you get a whole scatter of dots marching across the page.
And now look, the answer to my opening question is staring right at you. The dots climb in a perfectly straight, even line.

Here's an example from the chapter. We have data for a vehicle moving on a straight road. At zero seconds, the position is zero meters; at one second, twenty meters; at two seconds, forty meters; at three seconds, sixty meters; at four seconds, eighty meters; at five seconds, one hundred meters; and at six seconds, one hundred twenty meters. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Plot the position-time graph for a vehicle: (0s, 0m), (1s, 20m), (2s, 40m), (3s, 60m), (4s, 80m), (5s, 100m), (6s, 120m)|id=ex-q-1>>

First, we set up the axes. We show time along the X-axis and position along the Y-axis. For the scale, on the X-axis five divisions equal one second, and on the Y-axis five divisions equal twenty meters. <<WRITE_STEP:Axes: time on X-axis, position on Y-axis|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Scale: X-axis 5 divisions = 1 s; Y-axis 5 divisions = 20 m|id=ex-step-1-2>>
Now we plot the first point. At zero seconds the position is also zero meters, so this point is the origin itself. <<WRITE_STEP:At 0 s, position 0 m → plot at the origin|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Next, at one second the vehicle is at twenty meters. We find the point representing one second on the X-axis and draw a line parallel to the Y-axis. Then from twenty meters on the Y-axis we draw a line parallel to the X-axis. Where these two lines intersect is the position twenty meters at time one second. <<WRITE_STEP:At 1 s, draw line parallel to Y-axis; from 20 m, line parallel to X-axis; intersection = point (1 s, 20 m)|id=ex-step-1-4>>

We plot all the remaining points the same way: forty meters at two seconds, sixty meters at three seconds, eighty meters at four seconds, one hundred meters at five seconds, and one hundred twenty meters at six seconds. Then we connect all the points. <<WRITE_STEP:Similarly plot (2s,40m), (3s,60m), (4s,80m), (5s,100m), (6s,120m); connect all points|id=ex-step-1-5>>

And the answer is that the plotted points form a straight line. For this data, the position-time graph is a straight line, which tells us the motion is at constant speed. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The position-time graph is a straight line (constant-speed motion)|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. A vehicle starts from rest and speeds up, and we're given its position at different times. At zero seconds, the position is zero meters; at two seconds, one meter; at four seconds, four meters; at six seconds, nine meters; at eight seconds, sixteen meters; at ten seconds, twenty-five meters; and at twelve seconds, thirty-six meters. We need to plot the position-time graph for this. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Plot position-time graph for a vehicle starting from rest and speeding up|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by choosing a sensible scale so the points fit nicely on the page. On the X-axis, we let five divisions equal two seconds, and on the Y-axis, we let five divisions equal five meters. <<WRITE_STEP:X-axis: 5 divisions = 2 seconds|id=ex-step-1-1>><<WRITE_STEP:Y-axis: 5 divisions = 5 meters|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now we mark each pair of values. Time on the horizontal axis, position on the vertical axis. So we plot zero seconds at zero meters, two seconds at one meter, four seconds at four meters, and six seconds at nine meters. <<WRITE_STEP:Plot (0,0), (2,1), (4,4), (6,9)|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Then we continue marking the remaining points: eight seconds at sixteen meters, ten seconds at twenty-five meters, and twelve seconds at thirty-six meters. <<WRITE_STEP:Plot (8,16), (10,25), (12,36)|id=ex-step-1-4>>

Now look closely at the marked points. Unlike the case of uniform motion, these points do not fall on a straight line. Because the vehicle is speeding up, the position grows faster and faster, so when we join the points we get a curve. <<WRITE_STEP:Points do NOT lie on a straight line|id=ex-step-1-5>>
And the answer is: the position-time graph is a curve, not a straight line, showing that the vehicle is speeding up. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The points form a curve, not a straight line|id=ex-ans-1>>
A straight, evenly rising line means equal distance in equal time, the car is moving steadily, not speeding up and not slowing down. The picture told you in one second what the table hid.

So remember the recipe: time across the bottom, position up the side, and every row of the table becomes one point you read by going across then up. That's how numbers become a picture you can actually understand.

lesson_plans.title: Reading Motion from a Position-Time Graph

hook.text: If I showed you a graph of where a car was every second, could you tell me how fast it was going without ever seeing the car move?

crucial_facts: The steepness, or slope, of a position-time graph tells you the velocity: steeper means faster.
A straight line means constant velocity, while a curve means the velocity is changing.

diagrams.purpose: Show how the shape of a position-time graph encodes velocity: a straight line for steady speed and a curve for changing speed.

required_elements.description: Horizontal axis labelled Time in seconds, running left to right along the bottom.
Vertical axis labelled Position in meters, running up the left side.
A straight line rising at a constant slope from the origin, representing constant velocity.
A curve that starts shallow and gets steeper over time, representing increasing velocity.
A small right-triangle drawn under a segment of the straight line showing rise over run, distance over time.

choreography.narration: If I showed you a graph of where a car was every second, could you tell me how fast it was going, without ever seeing the car move?
<<SECTION:Position-time graphs|id=sec-1>>Let's build the graph that hides the answer. Along the bottom we put time, in seconds, and up the side we put position, in meters.
Every single point on this graph answers one plain question: where was the object at that moment in time? That alone is handy, but the real magic is in the shape.
Watch this straight line grow. <<WRITE_TEXT:Straight line drawn|id=text-1>>It climbs by the same amount of position in every equal slice of time.
Between two seconds and three seconds it climbs by twenty meters; between five seconds and six seconds it climbs by twenty meters again. Equal distance in equal time means the velocity never changes.
So here is the first big idea: a straight line on a position-time graph means constant velocity.
But that answers where and whether it's steady. How does the graph tell us how fast? Look at this little triangle tucked under the line.
<<SECTION:Slope is velocity|id=sec-2>>The height of the triangle is the distance covered, and the base is the time taken. Distance divided by time is exactly velocity.
<<WRITE_KEY:Slope of position-time graph equals velocity|id=key-1>>So the steepness of the line is the velocity. A steeper line means the object is moving faster.
Now what happens if the velocity itself keeps changing? Watch this second graph bend.
It starts shallow, then gets steeper and steeper. A shallow part means slow, a steep part means fast, so a curve that's bending upward is an object speeding up.
So remember the two shapes: a straight line is steady velocity, and a curve is changing velocity. Read the steepness and you've read the speed, no car required.

equations.explanation_in_words: Velocity is the distance covered, the height of our triangle, divided by the time taken, the base of our triangle.

lesson_plans.title: Velocity-Time Graphs: Reading Motion from a Line

hook.text: Three cars are driving. One holds steady, one speeds up, one slows down. Without seeing a single car, I can tell you exactly which is which just by looking at one line on a graph. Want to know the trick?

crucial_facts: The slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration: a steep line means fast change, a flat line means no change.
The area under a velocity-time graph is the distance travelled.

diagrams.purpose: Show how the slope of the velocity-time line distinguishes steady, speeding-up, and slowing-down motion, and how the area underneath gives distance.

required_elements.description: Horizontal axis labelled Time in seconds, running along the bottom.
Vertical axis labelled Velocity in metres per second, running up the left side.
A horizontal line at a constant velocity, parallel to the time axis, representing steady motion.
A straight line sloping upward from the origin, representing constant acceleration from rest.
A straight line sloping downward, starting high on the velocity axis, representing constant deceleration.
A small right-triangle drawn under the rising line showing rise over run, the slope that equals acceleration.
The shaded region between the rising line and the time axis, representing distance travelled.

choreography.narration: Three cars are driving. One holds steady, one speeds up, one slows down, and from a single line on a graph I can tell you exactly which is which.
<<SECTION:Velocity-time graphs|id=sec-1>>Here is the idea: we put time along the bottom and velocity going up the side, and then we just plot how fast the car is going at each moment.
Take the first car, cruising at a steady twenty metres per second. Its velocity never changes, so as time passes the line stays at the same height.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Flat line means steady velocity|id=text-1>>A flat line, parallel to the time axis, means steady velocity. No speeding up, no slowing down.
Now the second car starts from rest and speeds up steadily, gaining the same amount of velocity every second. Watch what its line does.
It slopes upward in a straight line. The third car begins fast and slows down steadily, so its line slopes downward instead.
So here is the real question: the steep line and the gentle line both slope up, but what is the slope actually telling us?
<<WRITE_KEY:Slope of v-t graph = acceleration|id=key-1>>The slope is the acceleration. Rise over run is change in velocity divided by change in time, and that is exactly what acceleration means.
A steep line means velocity changes quickly, so large acceleration. A flat line has zero slope, so zero acceleration. A downward slope means negative acceleration, slowing down.
<<SECTION:Distance from the graph|id=sec-2>>But the graph hides a second secret. Look at the space underneath the line, between the line and the time axis.

Here's an example from the chapter. Picture a car moving in a straight line along a highway at a steady velocity of seventy-two kilometers per hour, which is the same as twenty meters per second. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A car moves in a straight line at a steady velocity of 72 km/h (20 m/s). What does its velocity-time graph look like?|id=ex-q-1>>

Since the velocity never changes, we plot the velocity on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis, and keep the value pinned at twenty meters per second for every instant. <<WRITE_STEP:Velocity stays fixed at 20 m/s for all time t|id=ex-step-1-1>> That means the graph is a flat horizontal line sitting at twenty meters per second, parallel to the time axis. <<WRITE_STEP:Graph: horizontal line at v = 20 m/s|id=ex-step-1-2>>

And the answer is that the velocity-time graph is a straight horizontal line at twenty meters per second, showing the car keeps a constant velocity with zero acceleration. <<WRITE_ANSWER:A horizontal line at 20 m/s (72 km/h), constant velocity, zero acceleration|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Consider a car that starts from rest at zero meters per second, and its velocity increases steadily with time. At five seconds the velocity is two point five meters per second, at ten seconds it's five point zero meters per second, and at fifteen seconds it's seven point five meters per second. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A car starts from rest; velocity rises 0, 2.5, 5.0, 7.5, 10.0, 12.5, 15.0 m/s at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 s. Describe its v-t graph.|id=ex-q-1>>

Let's look at the rest of the readings. At twenty seconds the velocity is ten point zero meters per second, at twenty-five seconds it's twelve point five meters per second, and at thirty seconds it reaches fifteen point zero meters per second. Notice the pattern: in every five-second interval the velocity goes up by exactly two point five meters per second. <<WRITE_STEP:Every 5 s, velocity rises by a fixed 2.5 m/s|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Because the velocity increases by equal amounts in equal times, when we plot these points and join them we get an upward-sloping straight line. A straight line on a velocity-time graph means the acceleration is constant. So the answer is: this car moves with constant acceleration, and its velocity-time graph is an upward straight line. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Constant acceleration — the v-t graph is an upward straight line|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Consider a car moving with a velocity of fifteen point zero meters per second, whose velocity steadily decreases with time. At zero seconds it's fifteen point zero meters per second, at five seconds it's twelve point five meters per second, at ten seconds it's ten point zero meters per second, at fifteen seconds it's seven point five meters per second. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A car slows from 15.0 m/s; plot its velocity-time graph and find the acceleration.|id=ex-q-1>>

The velocity keeps dropping. At twenty seconds it's five point zero meters per second, at twenty-five seconds it's two point five meters per second, and at thirty seconds the velocity is zero. Notice the velocity falls by the same amount, two point five meters per second, in every five-second interval. <<WRITE_STEP:Each 5 s interval: velocity drops by 2.5 m/s|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Equal drops in equal times means the acceleration is constant, and since the velocity is decreasing, the acceleration points opposite to the motion. The velocity-time graph is a straight line sloping downward, from fifteen point zero meters per second at zero seconds to zero at thirty seconds. The slope gives the acceleration: a change of negative fifteen meters per second over thirty seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (0 - 15.0) / (30 - 0) = -0.5|id=ex-step-1-2>>

And the answer is a constant acceleration of negative zero point five meters per second squared, shown as a straight downward line on the velocity-time graph. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Acceleration = -0.5 m/s^2 (constant, straight downward line)|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. From our velocity-time graph, at ten seconds the velocity is five meters per second, and at twenty seconds the velocity is ten meters per second. Let's find the average acceleration over that interval. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the average acceleration between 10 s and 20 s, where v = 5 m/s at 10 s and v = 10 m/s at 20 s|id=ex-q-1>>
Remember, the slope of a velocity-time graph gives the acceleration. So we take the change in velocity divided by the change in time. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}|id=ex-eq-1>>

Substituting the values from the graph, the velocity goes from five meters per second up to ten meters per second, and the time goes from ten seconds to twenty seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (10 m/s − 5 m/s) / (20 s − 10 s)|id=ex-step-1-1>>
Now we work out the differences. The change in velocity is five meters per second, and the change in time is ten seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:a = 5 m/s / 10 s|id=ex-step-1-2>>
Dividing five meters per second by ten seconds, the result is zero point five meters per second squared. <<WRITE_ANSWER:a = 0.5 m/s² (meters per second squared)|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. We take the velocity-time graph from figure four point seventeen e, which is the same as figure four point seventeen c, and we follow the same steps we just used to read acceleration off a graph. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the average acceleration from the velocity-time graph in Fig. 4.17e (same as Fig. 4.17c).|id=ex-q-1>>

Following those steps on this graph, we compute the slope of the line and we obtain the average acceleration to be negative zero point five meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Average acceleration = slope of the v-t graph = -0.5 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-1>>

So what does that minus sign tell us? The minus sign indicates that the direction of acceleration is opposite to the direction of velocity, because the velocity is decreasing. The object is slowing down. And so the answer is an average acceleration of negative zero point five meters per second squared. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Average acceleration = -0.5 m/s^2 (acceleration opposes velocity; object slows down)|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. We have an object moving with a constant velocity of twenty meters per second for a time interval of six seconds, and we want the displacement using the velocity-time graph. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the displacement for constant velocity 20 m/s over 6 s using the v-t graph|id=ex-q-1>>

Because the velocity is constant, the graph is a flat horizontal line, and the region under it is a rectangle. The height of that rectangle is the velocity, twenty meters per second, and the width is the time interval, six seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:Area under v-t graph = rectangle (height = velocity, width = time)|id=ex-step-1>>
The key idea is that the area under the velocity-time graph equals the displacement. So area equals velocity times time interval. <<WRITE_STEP:Displacement = area = velocity x time|id=ex-step-2>>
Now we substitute the values from the graph. Twenty meters per second times six seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:Displacement = 20 m/s x 6 s|id=ex-step-3>>

Multiplying those together gives one hundred twenty meters. So the displacement between zero seconds and six seconds is one hundred twenty meters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Displacement = 120 meters|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. On a velocity-time graph, we want the displacement between ten seconds and twenty seconds, the part of the line running from point A to point B. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the displacement from 10 s to 20 s on the velocity-time graph (region ABDE).|id=ex-q-1>>

The displacement is simply the area under the line over that interval. That area, region A B D E, splits neatly into two pieces: a rectangle underneath, and a triangle sitting on top. <<WRITE_STEP:displacement = area of rectangle ACDE + area of triangle ABC|id=ex-step-1-1>>

First the rectangle. Its height is five meters per second and its width is the ten-second interval from ten seconds to twenty seconds. Five meters per second times ten seconds gives fifty meters. <<WRITE_STEP:rectangle = 5 m/s times 10 s = 50 m|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now the triangle on top. Its base is ten seconds and its height is five meters per second, so its area is one half times ten seconds times five meters per second, which is twenty-five meters. <<WRITE_STEP:triangle = one half times 10 s times 5 m/s = 25 m|id=ex-step-1-3>>
Adding the two pieces, fifty meters plus twenty-five meters, the total displacement is seventy-five meters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:displacement = 50 m + 25 m = 75 m|id=ex-ans-1>>
<<WRITE_KEY:Area under v-t graph = distance|id=key-2>>That shaded area is the distance travelled. Velocity multiplied by time is distance, and that product is exactly the area under the line.
So from one line you read everything: the height is how fast, the slope is the acceleration, and the area underneath is how far it has gone.

equations.explanation_in_words: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time it took, which is the rise over the run of the line.
Distance is velocity multiplied by time, and that is the area of the region under the line.

lesson_plans.title: Reading Motion Off a Velocity-Time Graph

hook.text: If I told you only how fast a car started, how hard it sped up, and for how long, could you tell me exactly where it ends up? Turns out, yes — and you don't need anything else.

crucial_facts: When acceleration is constant, the velocity-time graph is a straight line, and its slope IS the acceleration.
The area under a velocity-time graph equals the displacement — the distance you actually travel.

diagrams.purpose: Show that constant acceleration gives a straight velocity-time line whose slope is acceleration and whose enclosed area is displacement.

required_elements.description: Vertical axis labelled velocity, in meters per second.
Horizontal axis labelled time, in seconds.
Straight sloped line starting at initial velocity u on the velocity axis and rising to final velocity v at time t.
Point where the line meets the velocity axis at height u, the starting velocity.
Point on the line at time t, at height v, the final velocity.
Right-triangle showing rise (v minus u) over run (t), marking the slope of the line.
Rectangle of height u under the line, representing the u times t part of displacement.
Triangle on top of the rectangle, representing the extra one half a t squared displacement.

choreography.narration: If I told you only how fast a car started, how hard it sped up, and for how long, could you tell me exactly where it ends up? You actually can — and one straight line on a graph holds the whole answer.

<<SECTION:Constant acceleration|id=sec-1>>Here's the setup that makes everything simple: the car speeds up at a steady, constant rate. Not faster here and slower there — the same gain in speed every single second.
Let's draw its velocity against time. It starts at some speed u, and because the acceleration never changes, the line climbs perfectly straight up to a final speed v at time t.

<<WRITE_KEY:Constant acceleration means a straight v-t line; its slope is a|id=key-1>>And that straightness is the whole secret. A constant acceleration is exactly what makes the line straight, and the steepness of the line is the acceleration itself.
Look at this little triangle. The line rises by v minus u, over a run of t seconds. Rise over run — that's the slope, and the slope is the acceleration a.
<<WRITE_STEP:a equals (v minus u) divided by t|id=step-1>>So acceleration equals v minus u, all divided by t. Multiply across by t and rearrange, and you get your first kinematic equation.
That gives v equals u plus a t. It says: take your starting speed, add how much speed you gained, and that's how fast you're going. Clean.
But speed isn't distance. So here's the real question: how far did the car actually travel? That answer is hiding somewhere on this same graph.
<<WRITE_KEY:Area under a v-t graph equals displacement|id=key-2>>It's the area underneath the line. Velocity times time is distance, and that product is exactly the area sitting under the graph.
Split that area into two pieces you already know. A rectangle of height u — that's the distance u times t you'd cover at constant speed.

<<WRITE_STEP:s equals u t plus one half a t squared|id=step-2>>And a triangle on top — the extra distance from speeding up, which works out to one half a t squared. Add them and you get the second equation: displacement equals u t plus one half a t squared.

<<SECTION:Linking it all|id=sec-2>>So everything came from one straight line. Its slope handed you the acceleration; its area handed you the distance. Two pictures, two equations — and from those, you can always find whatever you're missing.

equations.explanation_in_words: Take your starting speed and add the speed you gained, which is acceleration multiplied by time.
The distance is the rectangle of steady-speed travel plus the triangle of extra distance from speeding up.

lesson_plans.title: Motion in a Plane: Two Things at Once

hook.text: Kick a football into the air. It rises, it moves forward, and it curves back down. So tell me, how does the ball know how to do two things at once?

crucial_facts: Motion in a plane is just two independent straight-line motions happening at the same time, one across and one up-down.
The sideways motion and the up-down motion don't interfere with each other; each obeys its own rules separately.

diagrams.purpose: Show that the curved arc of a kicked ball is the combination of a steady forward motion and a separate up-down motion governed by gravity.

required_elements.description: The curved arc path of the kicked ball through the air.
The initial launch velocity of the ball.
The steady horizontal velocity, unchanged at the top of the arc.
The downward pull of gravity acting on the ball.
The ground the ball is launched from and lands on.

choreography.narration: Kick a football into the air. It rises, it moves forward, and then it curves back down to the grass. So how does the ball know how to do two things at once?
Until now you've thought about motion along a single straight line, a car going forward, or a ball dropping straight down.
But look around you. A car overtaking on the highway shifts sideways as it moves forward. A satellite curves round and round the Earth. Almost nothing real stays on one line.
<<SECTION:Motion in a Plane|id=sec-1>>This kind of motion, spread out over a flat surface instead of a single line, is what we call motion in a plane, or motion in two dimensions.
Here's the secret the ball already knows. Watch the forward part of its motion all by itself.
Sideways, the ball just drifts forward at a steady pace. Nothing pushes or pulls it forward or back, so that part never speeds up and never slows down.
Now watch only the up-and-down part. Gravity tugs it, so it climbs, slows, stops for an instant, and falls, exactly like a ball thrown straight up.
So which one wins, the steady forward drift or the up-and-down tug of gravity?

<<WRITE_KEY:Motion in a plane = two independent straight-line motions at once|id=key-1>>Neither wins. They simply happen together, and neither one disturbs the other. The forward drift and the gravity-fall run side by side, completely independent.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Across: steady. Up-down: gravity. Combine into the arc.|id=text-1>>And when you let those two simple straight-line motions combine, the curved arc appears all on its own.
That's the whole trick. A complicated two-dimensional path is never as hard as it looks, because we can always split it into two ordinary straight-line motions.
Handle the across-motion with the rules you already know, handle the up-down motion the same way, and the plane takes care of itself.

lesson_plans.title: Uniform Circular Motion: Going Round and Round

hook.text: Here's something strange: you can run a full lap around a track, get totally exhausted, and yet your displacement is exactly zero.

crucial_facts: After one full revolution the distance equals the circumference, two times pi times R, but the displacement is zero.
In uniform circular motion the speed stays constant while the velocity keeps changing, because the direction keeps changing.

diagrams.purpose: Show the difference between the curved distance along the circle and the straight-line displacement, and set up one full revolution.

required_elements.description: A circle representing the merry-go-round path, centre marked, radius R shown.
Start point A on the circle.
End point C on the circle, roughly a quarter or third of the way around from A.
The curved arc from A through B to C, highlighting the actual distance travelled.
The straight line from A to C representing displacement.
A radius line from centre to the circle labelled R.
An arrow tangent to the circle showing instantaneous velocity direction at a point.

choreography.narration: Here's something strange: you can run a full lap around a track, get totally exhausted, and yet your displacement is exactly zero.
<<SECTION:Distance versus displacement|id=sec-1>>Picture a child on a merry-go-round, starting at point A and curving around to point C.
The distance they travel is the curved path they actually trace, all the way along the arc from A to C.
But their displacement is just the straight line connecting where they started to where they ended.
So can these two ever be wildly different? Watch what happens when the child goes all the way around once, back to A.

<<WRITE_KEY:One full lap: distance equals two pi R, displacement equals zero|id=key-1>>The distance is now the whole circumference, two times pi times R, but the displacement is zero, because they ended up exactly where they began.
That's the strange truth from the start: a full lap costs you real distance, yet your displacement comes out to nothing.
<<SECTION:Average speed around the loop|id=sec-2>>If the whole trip takes a time T, the average speed is just the circumference divided by that time.
<<WRITE_TEXT:uniform = constant speed|id=text-1>>Now suppose the child keeps a steady pace the whole way round. We call that uniform circular motion: circular motion at constant speed.
But here's the catch. At every instant the velocity points along the circle, tangent to it, like this.
If the speed never changes, is the velocity also unchanging? Watch the arrow as the child moves around.

Here's an example from the chapter. An object moves on a circular path of radius R, and it completes one full revolution, going round the circle exactly once. It takes a time T to make that one revolution. We want the average speed and the average velocity. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Object goes once around a circle of radius R in time T. Find average speed and average velocity.|id=ex-q-1>>

Let's start with the distance. In one full revolution the object traces out the entire boundary of the circle, so the distance travelled equals the circumference, which is two times pi times R. Now look at the displacement: after one revolution the object comes back to its original position, so the displacement after one revolution is zero. <<WRITE_STEP:Distance in one revolution = circumference = 2 pi R|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Displacement after one revolution = 0|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Average speed is distance divided by time, so the average speed equals two times pi times R divided by T. But average velocity is displacement divided by time, and since the displacement is zero, the average velocity equals zero. So the average speed is two times pi times R over T, while the average velocity is zero. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Average speed = 2 pi R / T ; Average velocity = 0|id=ex-ans-1>>

<<WRITE_KEY:Constant speed, changing velocity, because direction changes|id=key-2>>No. The arrow keeps swinging to a new direction at every point, so even with constant speed, the velocity is constantly changing.
And that's the heart of it: in uniform circular motion the speed stays fixed while the velocity changes, simply because the direction keeps turning.

equations.explanation_in_words: The average speed for one trip around is just the whole distance, the circumference, divided by the time it takes to go round once.

segments.raw_narration: Here's an example from the chapter. A bus is moving on a long straight highway. First, the driver presses the accelerator for ten seconds, and the velocity rises from thirty-six kilometers per hour, which is ten meters per second, up to fifty-four kilometers per hour, which is fifteen meters per second. Then later, the driver presses the brakes and the bus comes to a stop in five seconds. We want the average acceleration in both intervals. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the average acceleration when the accelerator is pressed, and when the brakes are pressed.|id=ex-q-1>>

We want the average acceleration in both intervals. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the average acceleration when the accelerator is pressed, and when the brakes are pressed.|id=ex-q-1>>

segments.raw_narration: Let's handle part one, when the accelerator is pressed. Here the initial velocity u is ten meters per second, the final velocity v is fifteen meters per second, and the time t is ten seconds. segments.raw_narration: So a equals fifteen meters per second minus ten meters per second, all divided by ten seconds. That gives five meters per second over ten seconds, which is zero point five meters per second squared. Since the magnitude of the velocity is increasing, this acceleration acts in the direction of the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (15 - 10) / 10 = 5 / 10 = 0.5 m/s^2, along velocity|id=ex-step-2>>

segments.raw_narration: So a equals zero meters per second minus fifteen meters per second, all over five seconds. topics.orig_book_content:
4.1 Motion in a Straight Line
You have learnt that when an object moves in a straight line, its motion is 
called linear motion. It can also be called motion in a straight line. It is the 
simplest kind of motion. Have you noticed it around you, such as children 
in a swimming race, a vertically falling ball, a car moving along a straight 
stretch of a highway or a train moving on a straight track (Fig. 4.1)? 
Fig. 4.1: Objects in a straight line motion
To discuss about the motion of an object, you first need to describe its 
position at various instants of time.
topics.our_understanding: Let's start with the simplest kind of motion there is — moving in a straight line. When an object travels along a straight path, we call that linear motion, or motion in a straight line. You've seen this everywhere, even if you never gave it a name. Think about children swimming straight across a pool in a race, or a ball you drop that falls straight down toward the ground. Picture a car cruising along a flat, straight stretch of highway, or a train gliding along a straight track. All of these are examples of motion in a straight line. We call it the simplest kind of motion because there are no curves, no turns, no swerving — the object just moves forward or backward along one single line. That makes it the perfect place to begin our study of motion. Now here's the key idea I want you to carry forward. Before we can really talk about how something is moving, we first need a way to describe where it is. Where is the object right now? Where was it a moment ago? Where will it be in the next moment? In other words, to understand motion, we have to describe the position of the object at different instants of time. Position tells us the location of the object, and time tells us the moment we're talking about. When we pair these two together — knowing where something is at each point in time — we begin to build a complete picture of its motion. Notice that this is really a way of thinking. Motion isn't just one frozen snapshot; it's a story of position changing as time passes. If you know an object's position at one second, at two seconds, at three seconds, and so on, you can describe its entire journey. So as we go further into this chapter, keep this foundation in mind. We're going to take this simple straight-line motion and learn how to describe it carefully, using position and time as our two basic tools. Everything more complicated that you'll meet later — speed, velocity, acceleration — grows out of this one simple starting point. So make friends with the idea right now: to describe motion, first describe position, instant by instant, as time moves along.

events.text: Linear motion = motion along one straight line, forward or backward only
Position = where the object is on the line
To describe motion, first describe position at each instant of time

Next, we'll do exactly that. <<TRACE:motion-line>>

topics.orig_book_content:
4.1.1 Describing position
How do we describe the position of an object? For that, as you learnt earlier, 
we first need to specify a fixed point as the reference point. The distance 
and direction of the object with respect to the reference point, at any 
instant of time, describes the position of the object at that instant of time. 
Note that apart from the distance, we also specify the direction from the 
reference point in which the object is located to describe its position. And 
when do we say that an object is in motion? If the position of the object with 
respect to the reference point changes with time, the object is said to be
in motion. On the other hand, the object is said to be at rest if its position 
with respect to the reference point does not change with time.

To describe the position of an object, we also need to specify its 
direction. For the object moving in a straight line, the object can move only 
in one of the two directions — forward and backward. Thus, the direction

topics.our_understanding:
Let's start with a simple but important question: how do we describe where something is? Think about it. If I just say an object is twenty meters away, that's not enough. Twenty meters from what? And in which direction? So the very first thing we need is a fixed point that we agree to measure from. We call this the reference point. Once we have that reference point, we describe an object's position by stating two things: how far it is from the reference point, and in which direction it lies. Both pieces matter. Distance alone doesn't pin down where something is.

Now here's a natural follow-up. When do we say an object is moving? The answer is beautifully simple. If the position of the object, measured from our reference point, changes as time passes, then the object is in motion. And if its position stays the same with time, we say the object is at rest. So motion is really just about position changing over time, relative to something fixed.

Let's make this concrete with an athlete running on a straight track. We pick her starting point as the reference point, and we draw a straight line with distances marked along it. We call that starting point the origin, and we label it O. As she runs, we can capture her position at different moments. Imagine her position at one instant is at a point we call B, and at another instant at a point we call A, each at some distance along that line.

But remember, position needs direction too. When an object moves along a straight line, it can only go in one of two directions, forward or backward. So instead of writing out words, we use signs. Positions to the right of the reference point O are taken as positive, and positions to the left of O are taken as negative. That's a clever shortcut. A single number with a plus or minus sign now tells us both how far the object is and in which direction. So minus twenty meters means twenty meters to the left, and positive forty meters means forty meters to the right. Notice how much information one signed number can carry. This idea of a reference point, distance, and direction is the foundation for everything we'll do in describing motion.

position changes in time means motion

4.1.2 Distance travelled and displacement 
Suppose an athlete starts running from point O at time t = 0 s, reaches 
point B at t = 4 s, then reaches point A at t = 10 s, then runs back along the 
same path till point B reaching there at t = 16 s (Fig. 4.4). How much is the 
total distance travelled by the athlete between the starting and stopping 
positions? The total distance travelled is OA + AB = 100 m + 60 m = 160 m. 
Let us now think about the distance between the starting and the 
stopping positions of the athlete. It is OB = 40 m, which is different from 
the total distance travelled by the athlete. So, let us now define another 
quantity — displacement. 
Displacement is the net change in the position of an object between the 
two given instants of time. A complete description of physical quantities 
like displacement requires specifying both a direction and its numerical 
value (with units). The numerical value (with units) of such a physical 
quantity is called its magnitude. The magnitude of displacement is the 
distance between the object’s positions at the two instants. The direction 
of displacement is specified from the position at the first instant towards

topics.our_understanding:
Let's get clear on two ideas that sound similar but mean different things: distance travelled and displacement. Imagine an athlete who starts at a point we'll call O. She runs forward, reaches a point B, keeps going to point A, and then turns around and runs back partway, ending up at B again. Now ask yourself, how much ground did her feet actually cover? If she went from O all the way to A, that's one hundred meters, and then she ran back from A to B, that's another sixty meters. Add those up and you get one hundred sixty meters. That total ground covered is what we call the total distance travelled. It doesn't care which direction she went, it just adds up every bit of path her feet touched.

But now ask a different question. Where did she start, and where did she end up? She started at O and finished at B. The straight-line gap between those two spots is just forty meters. That straight gap, from where you began to where you finished, is the displacement. Notice it's much smaller than the distance travelled, because the back-and-forth running cancels out.

Here's a key point about displacement. It needs two pieces of information to be fully described. First, how big it is, which we call its magnitude, and that's just the distance between the start and end positions. Second, which way it points, its direction. So for our athlete, her displacement is forty meters in the positive direction. Distance travelled, on the other hand, only needs a number with units, no direction at all. Both are measured in meters, the SI unit.

Now here's something worth chewing on. The magnitude of displacement is always less than or equal to the total distance travelled, never greater. They're equal only when an object moves in one straight direction without ever turning back. The moment it doubles back, the distance keeps piling up while the displacement shrinks. And if the object returns exactly to where it started, like a ball thrown straight up and falling back down, the displacement becomes zero even though plenty of distance was covered. Think about that whenever you hear someone confuse the two, because the difference really matters.

events.text: Distance = total path covered. Displacement = straight-line change in position, with direction.
If she'd returned all the way to O, displacement = 0

4.1.3 Average speed and average velocity
You have learnt about average speed in an earlier grade. It tells us how 
fast or slow an object moves. The average speed of an object is the total 
distance travelled divided by the time interval during which this distance 
is covered. Thus,

Since distance travelled has no direction (but only a numerical value), 
the average speed, which is calculated from distance travelled, also has no 
direction but only a numerical value. 
If an object moving in a straight line travels equal distances in equal 
intervals of time (for all possible choices of time intervals), it is said to 
be in uniform motion in a straight line. In this case, the object moves at a 
constant speed. On the other hand, if the object travels unequal distances in 
equal intervals of time, then it is in non-uniform motion in a straight line. 
In this case, the object moves with increasing speed or decreasing speed, or 
a combination of both. If the distances travelled in the successive intervals 
of times are increasing, its speed is increasing.
The concept that an object’s speed is the distance travelled divided by the time 
taken is well-established, dating back to ancient times even in India, as seen 
in the treatise Aryabhatiya (5th century CE). The following problem, based on 
this concept, is from a comprehensive mathematical text, the Ganitakaumudi 
(14th century CE). 
Indiaʼs Scientific Contributions
Example 4.1: Consider two postmen. They start walking towards each 
other from a distance of 210 yojanas (Yojana is a unit of distance used in 
ancient India). One travels 9 yojanas per day and the other covers 5 yojanas 
per day. Can you determine in how many days they will meet each other?
Answer: 
Total of distance covered by each postman in one day = 9 yojanas + 5 yojanas 
= 14 yojanas.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about two ideas that sound similar but tell us different things: average speed and average velocity. You've met average speed before. It tells us how fast or slow something moves, and we find it by taking the total distance travelled and dividing it by the time taken. Notice that distance is just a number with no direction, so average speed is also just a number with no direction. If something moves in a straight line and covers equal distances in equal slices of time, no matter how you chop up those time slices, we call that uniform motion, and the speed stays constant. But if it covers unequal distances in equal time slices, that's non-uniform motion, where the speed is speeding up, slowing down, or some mix of both. If the distances keep getting bigger each interval, the speed is increasing. This idea that speed equals distance over time is ancient. In India it appears in the Aryabhatiya from the fifth century, and a lovely problem about two postmen comes from the Ganitakaumudi in the fourteenth century.

Now here's where velocity comes in. Speed tells you how fast, but it never tells you which way. In real life, direction often matters a lot. So we define average velocity as the change in position, also called displacement, divided by the time interval. We can write this as average velocity equals s over t, where s is displacement and t is time. The big difference is that velocity carries a direction. For motion in a straight line, we show direction using a plus sign or a minus sign. The SI unit for both speed and velocity is the same, metres per second, and we also often use kilometres per hour.

Think about this powerful idea of a rate of change. Whenever we divide how much something changes by the time it took, we get a rate. So average velocity is really the average rate of change of position with respect to time. Here's something that can surprise you. If you swim to the far end of a pool and back, you travelled real distance, so your average speed is not zero, but your displacement is zero because you ended where you started, so your average velocity is zero! That's the whole point of keeping these two ideas separate.

Back to start means zero displacement, so zero average velocity

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about acceleration. You know that feeling when a vehicle suddenly starts moving from rest, and you feel a jolt? Or when it suddenly stops and you lurch forward? That jolt is your body sensing a change in velocity. Acceleration is the physics word that captures how quickly velocity changes.

Here's the key idea. Average acceleration over a time interval is simply the change in velocity divided by the time interval. And change in velocity means the final velocity minus the initial velocity. So if a vehicle goes from one velocity to another over some seconds, you subtract the starting velocity from the ending velocity, then divide by the time taken. The unit we use is meters per second squared.

Now, acceleration has a direction, just like velocity and displacement. When an object is moving in a straight line and its speed is increasing, the acceleration points in the same direction as the velocity. But when the speed is decreasing, the acceleration points opposite to the velocity. That's why a negative answer in these problems usually means slowing down.

Here's a subtle but important point. Acceleration doesn't depend on how fast something is moving. It depends on how quickly the velocity is changing. So a bus zooming down a straight highway at a steady, constant velocity has zero acceleration, even though it's moving fast. No change in velocity means no acceleration.

There's another beautiful idea here too. Acceleration can come from a change in the size of the velocity, or a change in its direction, or both. So even if speed stays exactly the same, if the direction keeps changing, there's still acceleration. We'll meet that case later.

When the velocity increases or decreases by equal amounts in equal intervals of time, no matter which intervals you pick, we say the acceleration is constant. A wonderful example is an object dropped from a height. As it falls, its velocity grows by the same amount each second, giving a constant acceleration of about nine point eight meters per second squared. That's the acceleration due to Earth's gravity, and we call it g.

One last reminder. You're free to choose where your origin sits and which direction you call positive. But once you choose, stay consistent for the whole problem. Don't switch midway, or your signs will get tangled.

book_examples.verbatim_text: Example 4.3: A bus is moving on a long straight highway with a velocity of 36 km h–1. The driver presses the accelerator for a time interval of 10 s and velocity of the bus increases to 54 km h–1. For some time, the bus moves at a constant velocity. Then, the driver notices an obstacle on the road ahead and presses the brake. The bus comes to a stop in a time interval of 5 s. Find the average acceleration in the two time intervals, (i) when the accelerator was pressed, and (ii) when the brakes were pressed. Answer: (i) When the driver presses the accelerator, u = 36 km h–1 = 10 m s–1, v = 54 km h–1 = 15 m s–1, t = 10 s. Using Eq. (4.3c), a = (15 m s–1 − 10 m s–1) / 10 s = 5 m s–1 / 10 s = 0.5 m s–2. Since the magnitude of velocity of the bus is increasing, the acceleration is acting in the direction of velocity. (ii) When the driver presses the brake, u = 54 km h–1 = 15 m s–1, v = 0 m s–1, t = 5 s. Using Eq. (4.3c) again, a = (0 m s–1 − 15 m s–1) / 5 s = −15 m s–1 / 5 s = −3 m s–2. The minus sign indicates that the acceleration is acting opposite to the direction of velocity (since the magnitude of velocity of the bus is decreasing).

book_examples.verbatim_text: Example 4.4: As we learnt earlier, when an object is dropped from a height, it takes a straight vertical path downwards before touching the ground. While coming down, the velocity of the object increases as shown in Fig. 4.10 at different instants. Find the magnitude of the average acceleration of the object in every successive interval of a second. Is the average acceleration constant across all intervals? What is the direction of this average acceleration? Answer: The magnitude of the average acceleration in every successive interval is: average acceleration between 0 s and 1 s = (9.8 − 0 m s–1)/(1−0 s) = 9.8 m s–2; average acceleration between 1 s and 2 s = (19.6 − 9.8 m s–1)/(2−1 s) = 9.8 m s–2; average acceleration between 2 s and 3 s = (29.4 − 19.6 m s–1)/(3−2 s) = 9.8 m s–2; average acceleration between 3 s and 4 s = (39.2 − 29.4 m s–1)/(4−3 s) = 9.8 m s–2. We note that the average acceleration is constant and equal to 9.8 m s–2. As the velocity is increasing in the direction of motion, the acceleration is in the direction of motion. This acceleration is called the acceleration due to gravitational force by the Earth and is denoted by g.
