topics.standalone_narration_text: Why does your body lurch forward the instant a bus slams its brakes, even though nothing actually pushed you? <<PAUSE:long>> That jolt you feel is your body sensing something change very fast: its velocity. One moment you were moving, the next you nearly weren't. <<PAUSE:short>> The physics word for how quickly velocity changes is acceleration. The bigger the jolt, the more violent the acceleration. <<SECTION:Average acceleration|id=sec-1>>So here is the heart of it: average acceleration is just how much the velocity changed, divided by how long it took to change. <<PAUSE:short>> Change in velocity means the velocity you ended with minus the velocity you started with. If you started at rest and ended fast, that change is large. <<WRITE_TEXT:change in velocity over time taken|id=text-1>>Now squeeze that big change into a tiny time, and you get a huge acceleration. Squeeze it into a long time, and the acceleration is gentle. <<WRITE_KEY:a equals change in velocity divided by time|id=key-1>>In plain words: take the final velocity, subtract the initial velocity, then divide by the time interval. That single number is the average acceleration. <<PAUSE:short>> Average acceleration is the final velocity minus the initial velocity, all divided by the time taken for that change. <<WRITE_EQUATION:a = \dfrac{v - u}{t_2 - t_1}|id=eq-1|boxed>> And because we divide a velocity, in meters per second, by a time in seconds, the unit comes out as meters per second squared. <<FOCUS:velocity-speeding>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:describing_motion_around_us:4_1_4:accel_direction_pair>> <<SECTION:Acceleration has direction|id=sec-2>>But here is the part people forget: acceleration is not just a number, it has a direction, just like velocity. When you are speeding up, the acceleration points the same way you are moving. Velocity and acceleration march together. <<POINT:accel-speeding>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:velocity-slowing>> So when does the acceleration point backwards, against your motion? Think about that braking bus. <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. A bus is moving on a long straight highway. First, the driver presses the accelerator for ten seconds, and the velocity rises from thirty-six kilometers per hour, which is ten meters per second, up to fifty-four kilometers per hour, which is fifteen meters per second. Then later, the driver presses the brakes and the bus comes to a stop in five seconds. We want the average acceleration in both intervals. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the average acceleration when the accelerator is pressed, and when the brakes are pressed.|id=ex-q-1>> Let's handle part one, when the accelerator is pressed. Here the initial velocity u is ten meters per second, the final velocity v is fifteen meters per second, and the time t is ten seconds. Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by time. <<WRITE_STEP:Part (i): u = 10 m/s, v = 15 m/s, t = 10 s|id=ex-step-1>> So a equals fifteen meters per second minus ten meters per second, all divided by ten seconds. That gives five meters per second over ten seconds, which is zero point five meters per second squared. Since the magnitude of the velocity is increasing, this acceleration acts in the direction of the velocity. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (15 - 10) / 10 = 5 / 10 = 0.5 m/s^2, along velocity|id=ex-step-2>> Now part two, when the brakes are pressed. Here the initial velocity u is fifty-four kilometers per hour, which is fifteen meters per second, the final velocity v is zero meters per second, and the time t is five seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:Part (ii): u = 15 m/s, v = 0 m/s, t = 5 s|id=ex-step-3>> So a equals zero meters per second minus fifteen meters per second, all over five seconds. That's negative fifteen meters per second divided by five seconds, which is negative three meters per second squared. The minus sign tells us the acceleration acts opposite to the direction of velocity, because the bus is slowing down. <<WRITE_STEP:a = (0 - 15) / 5 = -15 / 5 = -3 m/s^2, opposite to velocity|id=ex-step-4>> So the two answers are: zero point five meters per second squared in the direction of velocity when accelerating, and negative three meters per second squared, opposite to velocity, when braking. <<WRITE_ANSWER:(i) a = 0.5 m/s^2 (along velocity); (ii) a = -3 m/s^2 (opposite velocity)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. An object is dropped from a height and falls straight down along a vertical path. As it comes down, its velocity keeps increasing: at one second the velocity is nine point eight meters per second, at two seconds it's nineteen point six meters per second, at three seconds it's twenty-nine point four meters per second, and at four seconds it's thirty-nine point two meters per second. We want to find the magnitude of the average acceleration in every successive one-second interval. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A falling object has velocity 9.8, 19.6, 29.4, 39.2 m/s at t = 1, 2, 3, 4 s. Find the average acceleration in each interval.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the first interval, between zero seconds and one second. Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the change in time. So that's nine point eight minus zero meters per second, over one minus zero seconds, which gives nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 0 to 1 s: a = (9.8 - 0)/(1 - 0) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now the interval between one second and two seconds. The velocity goes from nine point eight to nineteen point six meters per second. So we take nineteen point six minus nine point eight, over two minus one seconds, and again we get nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 1 to 2 s: a = (19.6 - 9.8)/(2 - 1) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Continuing for the next two intervals: between two and three seconds, twenty-nine point four minus nineteen point six over one second is again nine point eight meters per second squared; and between three and four seconds, thirty-nine point two minus twenty-nine point four over one second is once more nine point eight meters per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Interval 2 to 3 s: a = (29.4 - 19.6)/(3 - 2) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-3>><<WRITE_STEP:Interval 3 to 4 s: a = (39.2 - 29.4)/(4 - 3) = 9.8 m/s^2|id=ex-step-1-4>> Notice that each one-second interval gives the same average acceleration of nine point eight meters per second squared, so the average acceleration is constant. And since the velocity is increasing in the direction of motion, the acceleration is in the direction of motion as well. This is the acceleration due to gravity, denoted by g, equal to nine point eight meters per second squared, directed downward in the direction of motion. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Average acceleration = 9.8 m/s^2, constant, in the direction of motion (g, due to gravity)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> When you slow down, the acceleration points opposite to your velocity, dragging your speed down. That backwards-pointing acceleration is exactly what threw you forward in your seat. <<POINT:accel-slowing>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So next time you feel that jolt, you will know: your body just measured an acceleration, and even felt which way it pointed.

4.2 Graphical Representation of Motion 
One useful way of representing motion can be a graphical 
representation. It provides a visual representation of how position, 
velocity, and acceleration change with time. Such graphs help in 
comparing the motion of two objects, in calculating physical quantities, 
or in identifying whether the motion is uniform or non-uniform. 
As you have learnt in Mathematics, graphs come in various forms, 
each suited to different types of data representation. To describe 
motion, we will use graphs to show dependence of one physical 
quantity, such as position, velocity or acceleration, on another 
quantity, such as time. Let us learn to plot and interpret line graphs 
for motion.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about a really powerful tool for studying motion: graphs. Up to now we've described motion with words and numbers, but a graph gives us a picture we can see at a glance. The idea is simple. We take two quantities that are connected, like position and time, and we draw how one changes as the other changes. So we might plot position against time, or velocity against time, or acceleration against time. Each kind of graph tells us a different story about how an object is moving.

Why bother with graphs at all? Because they make comparisons easy and they reveal patterns quickly. Imagine you have two cars and you want to know which one speeds up faster. If you sketch their velocity-time graphs side by side, you can see the answer right away without doing a single calculation. Graphs also let us calculate physical quantities directly from the lines and the areas underneath them, and they let us tell at a glance whether motion is uniform, meaning steady and unchanging, or non-uniform, meaning the speed keeps changing. That's a lot of information packed into a simple line.

Now, the textbook makes two important promises to keep things simple. First, in this whole chapter we'll only deal with cases where the acceleration is constant. That means the object speeds up or slows down at a steady, unchanging rate, which keeps our graphs neat and straight. Second, every graph here is for motion in a straight line moving in just one direction. In that special situation, some things that are usually different become equal. The distance travelled equals the size of the displacement, and the speed equals the size of the velocity. And there's a nice bonus: if the object starts at position zero when the clock reads zero, then the position-time graph looks exactly the same as the distance-time graph, and the velocity-time graph looks exactly the same as the speed-time graph.

There's also a small picture in this section worth imagining: an object dropped from a height. As it falls, its velocity keeps growing. After one second it's moving at nine point eight meters per second, after two seconds nineteen point six, after three seconds twenty-nine point four, and after four seconds thirty-nine point two meters per second. Notice how the velocity climbs by the same amount each second. That steady climb is exactly the kind of constant-acceleration motion we'll be drawing graphs of. So as we move forward, think of graphs as a visual language for motion, one we're about to learn to read and write.

We pick two things that are connected — say, position and time — and we draw how one changes as the other changes. Time runs along the bottom, position climbs up the side. That equal jump each second means the acceleration is constant. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Velocity increases by 9.8 m/s every second → acceleration is constant|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Time keeps marching on, but position never changes — so the line goes flat. topics.our_understanding:
Let's learn how to turn a table of numbers into a picture you can actually understand at a glance. That picture is called a graph. Imagine you have a vehicle moving along a straight road, and someone records where it is at each second. At zero seconds it's at zero meters, at one second it's at twenty meters, at two seconds forty meters, and so on, gaining twenty meters every second. Numbers in a table are useful, but a graph lets you see the motion.

Here's how we build one. Take graph paper, which is already divided into tiny squares, so plotting is neat and accurate. Draw two lines that cross each other at right angles. The point where they meet is called the origin. The horizontal line is the X-axis, and the vertical line is the Y-axis. Now we decide what goes where. For motion, we usually put time along the X-axis and position along the Y-axis.

Next comes the scale. We can't fit every meter onto a tiny square, so we choose a sensible rule. For example, five divisions equal one second on the time axis, and five divisions equal twenty meters on the position axis. A good scale spreads the data out nicely so it fills the available space without crowding.

Now we plot. For each row in the table, find the time on the X-axis and draw a faint line going up. Then find the position on the Y-axis and draw a faint line going across. Where those two lines meet is your point. Do this for every pair of values. When you connect the points for our steady vehicle, you get a beautiful straight line.

Notice something important here. Those points in between the marked ones aren't just decoration. They tell you where the vehicle would be at in-between times, but only if it's moving at a constant speed. If the speed changes, the in-between points behave differently, and the line bends into a curve instead of staying straight.

And one last thing to keep in your mind. A graph is not a route map. It doesn't show the road or which way the vehicle turned. It shows how the position changes with time, measured from the origin. That's the whole idea, and you'll use it again and again as you explore motion.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about what a position-time graph really tells us. On this kind of graph, time runs along the bottom, the horizontal axis, and position runs up the side, the vertical axis. So every point on the graph answers a simple question: where was the object at that moment in time? That's already useful, but the shape of the graph hides even more information.

Here's the first big idea. If the graph is a straight line going upward, that means the object covers equal amounts of distance in equal amounts of time. Imagine watching an object between two seconds and three seconds, and then again between five seconds and six seconds. If it moves the same twenty meters in each of those one-second stretches, its velocity is constant. A straight line means steady, unchanging velocity.

Now if the graph is curved instead of straight, the story changes. A curve means the object covers different amounts of distance in equal time intervals. Maybe it moves a little in one interval and much more in the next. That means its velocity is changing, and changing velocity is what we call accelerated motion.

So from the position-time graph we get position at any instant, and we can also pull out velocity. How? By looking at the slope, which is just the steepness of the line. Pick two points, A and B. Find how much the position changed between them, and how much the time changed between them. Divide the change in position by the change in time, and you get the average velocity. That's exactly what slope means: the rate at which the quantity on the vertical axis changes compared to the quantity on the horizontal axis.

Here's a concrete piece. If an object is at forty meters at two seconds and at eighty meters at four seconds, then position changed by forty meters while time changed by two seconds. Forty divided by two gives twenty meters per second. That's the velocity.

Keep this in mind: a steeper line means a faster object, because more position is being gained in the same time. And a flat horizontal line means the position never changes at all, so the object is simply sitting still. Reading these graphs is like reading the story of a journey just from its shape.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about velocity-time graphs. Just like a position-time graph shows how position changes over time, a velocity-time graph shows how velocity changes over time. We put time along the bottom and velocity going up the side, and the shape of the line tells us a lot about the motion.

Think about three different cars. The first one cruises along a highway at a steady twenty meters per second, which is the same as seventy-two kilometers per hour. Since its velocity never changes, its graph is a flat straight line, running parallel to the time axis. The second car starts from rest and speeds up steadily, gaining two and a half meters per second every five seconds. Its graph is a straight line sloping upward. The third car begins at fifteen meters per second and slows down steadily until it stops. Its graph is a straight line sloping downward.

Now here's the beautiful part. From a velocity-time graph you can pull out two more physical quantities. First, the slope of the line tells you how fast velocity is changing, and that is exactly the acceleration. A flat line has zero slope, so zero acceleration. An upward-sloping line means constant positive acceleration. A downward-sloping line means the acceleration points opposite to the velocity, so it gets a minus sign, and the object is slowing down.

Second, and this surprises people, the area between the line and the time axis gives you the displacement. For the steady car, that area is just a rectangle, velocity times time. For the accelerating car, the area is a rectangle plus a triangle, and you add those two pieces together.

So notice the lovely symmetry here. On a position-time graph, the slope gave us velocity. On a velocity-time graph, the slope gives us acceleration, and the area underneath gives us displacement. Reading a graph carefully lets you uncover quantities you might think you'd need a formula for. Once you're comfortable with this, we'll move on to the actual equations of motion.

Q: A car moves in a straight line at a steady velocity of 72 km/h (20 m/s). What does its velocity-time graph look like?
Velocity stays fixed at 20 m/s for all time t
Graph: horizontal line at v = 20 m/s
A horizontal line at 20 m/s (72 km/h), constant velocity, zero acceleration

Every 5 s, velocity rises by a fixed 2.5 m/s
Constant acceleration — the v-t graph is an upward straight line
Q: A car slows from 15.0 m/s; plot its velocity-time graph and find the acceleration.
Each 5 s interval: velocity drops by 2.5 m/s
Acceleration = -0.5 m/s^2 (constant, straight downward line)

a = 5 m/s / 10 s
a = 0.5 m/s² (meters per second squared)

Average acceleration = slope of the v-t graph = -0.5 m/s^2
Average acceleration = -0.5 m/s^2 (acceleration opposes velocity; object slows down)
Q: Find the displacement for constant velocity 20 m/s over 6 s using the v-t graph
Area under v-t graph = rectangle (height = velocity, width = time)
Displacement = area = velocity x time
Displacement = 20 m/s x 6 s
Displacement = 120 meters
Q: Find the displacement from 10 s to 20 s on the velocity-time graph (region ABDE).
displacement = area of rectangle ACDE + area of triangle ABC
rectangle = 5 m/s times 10 s = 50 m
triangle = one half times 10 s times 5 m/s = 25 m
displacement = 50 m + 25 m = 75 m

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about a very special and very useful kind of motion: moving in a straight line while speeding up or slowing down at a steady, constant rate. When acceleration is constant, the acceleration at every single instant is exactly the same as the average acceleration over any time interval. That simple fact lets us build three neat equations that describe everything about the motion.

We have five important quantities to keep track of: how far you go, which is displacement; how long it takes, the time; how fast you started, the initial velocity; how fast you end up, the final velocity; and how quickly your speed is changing, the acceleration. The three kinematic equations connect these five so that if you know some of them, you can always find the rest.

The first equation comes straight from the meaning of acceleration. Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by time. If you rearrange that, you get final velocity equals initial velocity plus acceleration times time. If you draw velocity against time, this is a straight, slanted line, and the slope of that line is the acceleration. The starting point of the line, where it touches the velocity axis, is your initial velocity.

The second equation comes from a clever idea: the displacement equals the area under that velocity-time graph. That area is a rectangle plus a triangle stacked together. When you work out those areas, you get displacement equals initial velocity times time, plus one half times acceleration times time squared.

The third equation is born by combining the first two and getting rid of time. After some algebra, you arrive at: final velocity squared equals initial velocity squared plus two times acceleration times displacement. This one is wonderful when you don't know the time but want to connect speeds and distance.

A word of caution. These equations only work when the acceleration stays constant. Also, when something moves in a straight line in one direction, distance and displacement are the same, and speed and velocity are the same. But when motion goes back and forth, the plus or minus signs on these quantities tell you the direction. Master these three equations, and you can predict where an object will be, or how fast it's going, at any future moment.

topics.orig_book_content:
4.4 Motion in a Plane
Motion in a plane, such as a vehicle overtaking another, the path of a 
kicked ball or a satellite moving in a circular path, is called motion in two 
dimensions (Fig. 4.21).
Fig. 4.21: Motion in a plane
topics.our_understanding:
So far, you've been thinking about motion that happens along a straight line, like a car going forward or a ball dropping straight down. But the world isn't that simple, is it? Most of the motion we see around us doesn't stay neatly on a single line. Think about a car overtaking another car on the highway. It doesn't just move forward, it also shifts sideways into the next lane, then back again. Or picture a football that someone kicks high into the air. It rises, moves forward, and then curves back down to the ground, tracing out a graceful arc. Or imagine a satellite circling the Earth, going round and round in a curved path. All of these are examples of motion that takes place on a flat surface, what we call a plane.

This kind of motion is called motion in two dimensions, and here's why that name makes sense. When something moves along a straight line, you only need one direction to describe where it is, just one dimension. But when motion spreads out across a flat surface, you need two directions to pin it down, like left-and-right combined with forward-and-backward, or up-and-down combined with sideways. That's two dimensions working together at the same time.

Why does this matter? Because real motion almost always involves more than one direction at once. The kicked ball is moving forward and upward at the same time. The overtaking car is moving forward and sideways at the same time. To truly describe how these things move, we can't just talk about one direction. We have to keep track of two directions together. Notice how this builds on what you already know. The ideas of distance, displacement, speed, and velocity don't get thrown away. They simply get richer, because now they have to account for motion happening in two directions at once. As you go further, you'll learn how to break this two-dimensional motion into pieces, looking at each direction separately, which makes it much easier to understand. For now, just hold onto this picture in your mind: a ball arcing through the air, a car sweeping across lanes, a satellite looping around the Earth. That's motion in a plane.

events.text: Motion in a plane = two independent straight-line motions at once
Across: steady. Up-down: gravity. Combine into the arc.

A complicated two-dimensional path is never as hard as it looks, because we can always split it into two ordinary straight-line motions. <<PAUSE:short>> Handle the across-motion with the rules you already know, handle the up-down motion the same way, and the plane takes care of itself. <<POINT:ground>>

4.4.1 Uniform circular motion
Do you remember learning about circular motion in an earlier grade? 
When an object moves in a circular path, its motion is called circular 
motion.
Suppose a child is sitting on a moving merry-go-around. The child, 
moving on a circular path, moves from A to B to C as shown in Fig. 4.22. 
What is the distance travelled by the child? What is their displacement from 
their original position? The distance travelled by the child is the curve ABC 
and displacement is the straight-line AC. As you can see both are not equal. 
What is the distance travelled by the child in making one revolution 
(going round the circle once)? It is equal to the circumference of the circle. 
So, if the radius of the circular path is R, the distance travelled by the child 
in making one revolution is 2 R. On the other hand, the displacement is 
zero, since the child comes back to its original position after making one 
revolution.

Imagine an athlete running along a closed path. In Fig. 4.23a, the athlete 
follows a rectangular track (ABCD), running at a uniform speed on the

times to complete one round. In Fig. 4.23b, the athlete is running along

complete one round. What happens if we go on increasing the number of 
sides indefinitely? As the number of sides increases, the athlete has to take 
turns more and more frequently. Finally, the track approaches a circle, 
with each side decreasing to a point and the direction of athlete’s velocity 
changes continuously.

speed and a circular path — are often not met. So, uniform circular motion

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about going in circles. When an object moves along a circular path, we call that circular motion. Picture a child sitting on a merry-go-round. As they spin from one point to another and around, two questions come up: how far did they travel, and how far are they from where they started? Those are very different things. The distance is the curved path they actually trace along the circle. The displacement is the straight line connecting their start and end points. These two are not equal.

Now here's a neat result. If the child goes all the way around once, the distance they travel equals the circumference of the circle. So if the radius is R, the distance for one full trip around is two times pi times R. But their displacement after one complete revolution is zero, because they end up right back where they started. So if it takes a time T to go around once, the average speed is two times pi times R, divided by T. The average velocity, though, is zero, because the displacement is zero.

Now let's add a special condition. When the object moves around the circle at a constant, unchanging speed, we call this uniform circular motion. The speed stays the same at every point. But here's the deep question: even though the speed is constant, is the velocity constant? No! Velocity has both a size and a direction. The direction keeps changing as you go around.

To see why, imagine an athlete running a rectangular track. They change direction four times. On a hexagonal track, six times. As you add more and more sides, the turns happen more often, and eventually the shape becomes a circle, where the direction changes smoothly and continuously at every instant. The velocity at any point points along the tangent to the circle, in the direction of motion. There's a lovely activity with a marble spinning inside a ring: lift the ring, and the marble shoots off in a straight line, in whatever direction it was heading at that instant.

And here's the key insight: because the direction of velocity keeps changing, the velocity itself is changing, which means there is acceleration. Even with constant speed, uniform circular motion is accelerated motion. In everyday life we forget that a change in direction alone counts as acceleration. This is an idealised model, but it's the foundation for understanding planets orbiting the Sun and vehicles taking circular turns.

questions.q_text: Which of the following is the best example of motion in a straight line?
options: A. A car going around a roundabout
B. A ball dropped straight down toward the ground
C. A merry-go-round spinning
D. A boomerang curving through the air

questions.q_text: According to the lesson, what two basic things do we pair together to build a complete picture of an object's motion?
options: A. Speed and acceleration
B. Force and mass
C. Position and time
D. Distance and weight

questions.q_text: Why is motion in a straight line described as the simplest kind of motion?
options: A. Because the object never moves at all
B. Because there are no curves, turns, or swerving — the object moves along one single line
C. Because it always happens very slowly
D. Because it only happens to very small objects

questions.q_text: The lesson says motion is not just one frozen snapshot. What does it compare motion to instead?
options: A. A single photograph
B. A story of position changing as time passes
C. A list of forces acting on the object
D. A fixed point that never moves

questions.q_text: A toy car is observed on a straight track. At 1 second it is at the start line, at 2 seconds it is a little further along, and at 3 seconds it is even further along. Explain how knowing these positions at these times lets us describe the car's motion, using the ideas from this lesson.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recognize that the car is moving along a straight track, so this is motion in a straight line — the simplest kind of motion, with no curves or turns. Step 2: Recall the key idea from the lesson: to describe motion, we must describe the position of the object at different instants of time. Position tells us where the car is, and time tells us the moment we are talking about. Step 3: Pair the position with the time at each instant. At 1 second the car is at the start line (one position-time pair), at 2 seconds it is further along (a second pair), and at 3 seconds it is further still (a third pair). Step 4: By stringing these snapshots together, we see the position is changing as time passes — the car keeps moving forward along the line. This sequence of positions at successive instants is exactly what the lesson means by motion being a 'story of position changing as time passes.' Step 5: Therefore, knowing the position of the car at each instant of time gives us a complete description of its journey along the straight track, which is the foundation for later ideas like speed and velocity.

questions.q_text: To fully describe the position of an object, which of the following must we state?
options: A. Only how far the object is from the reference point
B. Only the direction in which the object lies
C. Both the distance from the reference point and the direction
D. Only the time at which we observe the object

questions.q_text: Based on our definition, when do we say an object is in motion?
options: A. When the object is far from the reference point
B. When its position measured from the reference point changes with time
C. When the object is to the right of the origin
D. When its distance is a positive number

questions.q_text: If an object's position is given as minus fifteen meters, what does this tell us?
options: A. The object is fifteen meters to the right of the origin
B. The object is fifteen meters to the left of the origin
C. The object is moving backward at fifteen meters per second
D. The object is fifteen meters below the origin

questions.q_text: A book is placed on a table. Over five minutes, its distance from a fixed corner of the room stays exactly two meters in the same direction. Is the book at rest or in motion? Explain using the definition.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the reference point. Here it is the fixed corner of the room. Step 2: Recall the rule for motion. An object is in motion if its position, measured from the reference point, changes as time passes; it is at rest if its position stays the same with time. Step 3: Check the book's position. Its distance stays at two meters and the direction does not change over the five minutes, so its position does not change with time. Step 4: Conclusion. Since the position remains the same as time passes, the book is at rest.

questions.q_text: An athlete starts at the origin O on a straight track. We mark positions to the right as positive and to the left as negative. At one instant her position is positive forty meters, and at a later instant it is positive seventy meters. Is she in motion? In which direction did she move, and by how much did her position change?
questions.answer: Step 1: Compare the two positions. At the first instant she is at positive forty meters and at the later instant she is at positive seventy meters. Step 2: Apply the definition of motion. Her position has changed with time (from forty to seventy meters), so she is in motion. Step 3: Determine the direction. Both positions are positive, meaning to the right of O. The number increased from forty to seventy, so she moved further to the right, that is, in the positive (rightward) direction. Step 4: Find the change in position. Seventy meters minus forty meters equals thirty meters. So her position changed by thirty meters to the right.

questions.q_text: Which statement correctly describes the difference between distance travelled and displacement?
options: A. Distance needs a direction while displacement only needs a number
B. Displacement needs both a magnitude and a direction, while distance only needs a number with units
C. Distance and displacement are always equal
D. Displacement is always larger than distance travelled

questions.q_text: A ball is thrown straight up and falls back into the thrower's hand. What is its displacement?
options: A. Twice the height it reached
B. Equal to the height it reached
C. Zero
D. Greater than the distance travelled

questions.q_text: When is the magnitude of displacement exactly equal to the total distance travelled?
options: A. When the object turns around exactly once
B. When the object returns to its starting point
C. When the object moves in one straight direction without ever turning back
D. Never, displacement is always smaller

questions.q_text: An athlete starts at point O, runs straight to point A which is 100 meters away in the positive direction, then turns around and runs back 60 meters to point B. Find the total distance travelled and the magnitude of the displacement.
questions.answer: First, the total distance travelled adds up every bit of path covered, regardless of direction. From O to A is 100 meters, and from A back to B is 60 meters. Adding these gives 100 plus 60, which equals 160 meters. That is the total distance travelled. Next, the displacement is the straight-line gap between the start and end positions. She started at O and ended at B. Since A is 100 meters from O, and she came back 60 meters from A, her end position B is 100 minus 60, which equals 40 meters from O. So the magnitude of displacement is 40 meters, directed in the positive direction. Notice the displacement (40 meters) is smaller than the distance travelled (160 meters) because the back-and-forth running cancels out.

questions.q_text: A person walks 30 meters east, then walks 30 meters back west to return to the starting point. What is the total distance travelled and what is the displacement?
questions.answer: The total distance travelled is found by adding all path covered. Walking 30 meters east plus 30 meters west gives 30 plus 30, which equals 60 meters total distance. For displacement, we compare the start and end positions. The person walked 30 meters away and then 30 meters back, returning exactly to where they began. Since the start and end positions are the same point, the straight-line gap between them is zero. Therefore the displacement is 0 meters. This shows how distance can be large (60 meters) while displacement is zero when an object returns to its starting point.

questions.q_text: A swimmer swims to the far end of a pool and comes straight back to where they started. Which statement is true about their average speed and average velocity for the whole trip?
options: A. Both average speed and average velocity are zero
B. Average speed is zero but average velocity is not zero
C. Average speed is not zero but average velocity is zero
D. Both are equal and not zero

questions.q_text: What is the main difference between average speed and average velocity?
options: A. Average speed uses displacement while average velocity uses distance
B. Average velocity carries a direction while average speed does not
C. They have different SI units
D. Average speed can be negative but average velocity cannot

questions.q_text: An object moving in a straight line covers unequal distances in equal slices of time. What kind of motion is this?
options: A. Uniform motion
B. Non-uniform motion
C. Motion with zero displacement
D. Motion with constant velocity

questions.q_text: A car travels 150 kilometres in 3 hours. Calculate its average speed in kilometres per hour.
questions.answer: Average speed is found by dividing the total distance travelled by the time taken. Here the distance is 150 kilometres and the time is 3 hours. So average speed equals 150 divided by 3, which is 50 kilometres per hour.

questions.q_text: A runner jogs 400 metres east in 100 seconds, then turns around and jogs 400 metres back west in 100 seconds, ending exactly where they started. Find the average speed and the average velocity for the whole trip.
questions.answer: First find the total distance: the runner covered 400 metres going out plus 400 metres coming back, which is 800 metres. The total time is 100 seconds plus 100 seconds, which is 200 seconds. Average speed equals total distance over total time, so 800 divided by 200 equals 4 metres per second. Now find the displacement: the runner ended exactly where they started, so the change in position is zero metres. Average velocity equals displacement over time, so 0 divided by 200 equals 0 metres per second. So the average speed is 4 metres per second, but the average velocity is 0 metres per second.

questions.q_text: A bus travels down a straight highway at a steady velocity of 30 meters per second. What is its acceleration?
options: A. 30 meters per second squared
B. Zero
C. 9.8 meters per second squared
D. Cannot be determined without the time

questions.q_text: While moving in a straight line, an object has an acceleration that points opposite to its velocity. What does this tell us about the object?
options: A. It is speeding up
B. It is moving backward
C. It is slowing down
D. It has stopped

questions.q_text: A car goes around a circular track at a perfectly constant speed. Is it accelerating?
options: A. No, because its speed never changes
B. Yes, because its direction keeps changing
C. No, because acceleration requires a change in speed
D. Only at the start and end of the loop

questions.q_text: A car moving in a straight line increases its velocity from 8 meters per second to 20 meters per second in 4 seconds. Find its average acceleration.
questions.answer: Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time interval. The change in velocity is the final velocity minus the initial velocity: 20 minus 8 equals 12 meters per second. Divide this by the time of 4 seconds: 12 divided by 4 equals 3. So the average acceleration is 3 meters per second squared. The positive sign and the fact that it points in the direction of motion confirm the car is speeding up.

questions.q_text: A train traveling at 25 meters per second slows down to 5 meters per second in 10 seconds. Taking the direction of motion as positive, find the average acceleration and explain the sign.
questions.answer: Change in velocity is final minus initial: 5 minus 25 equals negative 20 meters per second. Divide by the time of 10 seconds: negative 20 divided by 10 equals negative 2 meters per second squared. So the average acceleration is negative 2 meters per second squared. The negative sign means the acceleration points opposite to the direction of motion, which makes sense because the train is slowing down.

questions.q_text: Why are velocity-time graphs especially useful when comparing how two cars speed up?
options: A. They show the exact color and size of each car
B. They let you see which car accelerates faster at a glance without calculations
C. They tell you the price of each car
D. They only work when both cars move at the same speed

questions.q_text: In this chapter, the graphs are kept neat and straight because of which assumption about the motion?
options: A. The acceleration is constant
B. The object never moves
C. The velocity is always zero
D. The object moves in a circle

questions.q_text: For motion in a straight line moving in just one direction, which statement is true?
options: A. Distance travelled is always greater than displacement
B. Speed is always less than the size of velocity
C. Distance travelled equals the size of the displacement
D. Velocity and acceleration are always equal

questions.q_text: Under what condition does the position-time graph look exactly the same as the distance-time graph?
options: A. When the object starts at position zero at time zero
B. When the object is at rest
C. When the acceleration is changing
D. When the object moves backward

questions.q_text: An object is dropped from a height. Its velocity is 9.8 meters per second after one second, 19.6 after two seconds, 29.4 after three seconds, and 39.2 after four seconds. By how much does the velocity increase each second, and what would its velocity be after five seconds?
questions.answer: Step 1: Find the change each second. From one second to two seconds the velocity goes from 9.8 to 19.6, an increase of 9.8 meters per second. Checking the next interval: 19.6 to 29.4 is also 9.8, and 29.4 to 39.2 is again 9.8. So the velocity increases by 9.8 meters per second every second. This steady increase is what constant acceleration means. Step 2: Predict the velocity after five seconds. Take the four-second value of 39.2 and add one more increase of 9.8: 39.2 plus 9.8 equals 49.0 meters per second. So after five seconds the object would be moving at 49.0 meters per second.

questions.q_text: On a graph, what do we call the point where the X-axis and the Y-axis cross each other?
options: A. The scale
B. The origin
C. The plot point
D. The axis

questions.q_text: Which of the following best describes what a position-versus-time graph actually shows you?
options: A. The exact road and turns the vehicle took
B. A route map of the journey
C. How the position changes with time, measured from the origin
D. The colour and shape of the vehicle

questions.q_text: If a vehicle's speed keeps changing instead of staying constant, what happens to the line on the position-versus-time graph?
options: A. It stays a perfectly straight line
B. It bends into a curve
C. It disappears
D. It becomes the X-axis

questions.q_text: Suppose five divisions on the position axis stand for twenty meters. If a vehicle is at sixty meters at a certain time, how many divisions up from the origin should you go to plot that position?
questions.answer: Step 1: Find out how many meters each division represents. Five divisions equal twenty meters, so one division equals twenty divided by five, which is four meters. Step 2: We need to plot sixty meters. Divide sixty meters by four meters per division: sixty divided by four equals fifteen. Step 3: So you go fifteen divisions up from the origin to plot the position of sixty meters.

questions.q_text: Using the steady vehicle from the lesson (zero meters at zero seconds, twenty meters at one second, forty meters at two seconds, gaining twenty meters every second), where on the graph would you plot the point for three seconds, and what is the position there?
questions.answer: Step 1: The vehicle gains twenty meters every second. At three seconds, the position is twenty meters times three, which equals sixty meters. Step 2: To plot it, find three seconds on the X-axis (the horizontal time axis) and draw a faint line going up. Step 3: Find sixty meters on the Y-axis (the vertical position axis) and draw a faint line going across. Step 4: Where those two faint lines meet is your point. Since the speed is constant, this point lies on the same straight line as all the others.

questions.q_text: On a position-time graph, what does a flat horizontal line tell you about the object?
options: A. The object is moving at constant high speed
B. The object is at rest, not changing position
C. The object is accelerating
D. The object is moving backward

questions.q_text: If a position-time graph is curved rather than a straight line, what can you conclude about the object's motion?
options: A. Its velocity is constant
B. It is standing still
C. Its velocity is changing, so it is accelerating
D. It covers equal distances in equal times

questions.q_text: Two objects are shown as straight lines on the same position-time graph. One line is steeper than the other. What does the steeper line indicate?
options: A. That object is slower
B. That object is faster
C. That object is at rest
D. That object is moving backward

questions.q_text: An object is at 30 meters at a time of 1 second, and at 90 meters at a time of 4 seconds. The position-time graph between these points is a straight line. Find the object's velocity.
questions.answer: Step 1: Find the change in position. The position goes from 30 meters to 90 meters, so the change is 90 minus 30, which equals 60 meters. Step 2: Find the change in time. Time goes from 1 second to 4 seconds, so the change is 4 minus 1, which equals 3 seconds. Step 3: The velocity is the slope, which is the change in position divided by the change in time. That is 60 meters divided by 3 seconds, which equals 20 meters per second. So the object's velocity is 20 meters per second.

questions.q_text: An object moves 10 meters during the first second, then 25 meters during the next second, then 40 meters during the third second. Would its position-time graph be a straight line or a curve, and what does this say about its motion?
questions.answer: Step 1: Check whether equal distances are covered in equal time intervals. In the first second it covers 10 meters, in the second it covers 25 meters, and in the third it covers 40 meters. These distances are not equal even though the time intervals are all one second each. Step 2: Since unequal distances are covered in equal times, the line cannot be straight; the graph must be a curve. Step 3: A curved position-time graph means the velocity is changing. Therefore the object is undergoing accelerated motion — in fact it is speeding up, since it covers more distance each successive second.

questions.q_text: On a velocity-time graph, what physical quantity does the slope of the line represent?
options: A. Displacement
B. Acceleration
C. Speed
D. Distance

questions.q_text: What does the area between the line and the time axis on a velocity-time graph tell you?
options: A. The acceleration
B. The average velocity
C. The displacement
D. The final velocity

questions.q_text: A velocity-time graph shows a flat straight line running parallel to the time axis. What does this tell you about the motion?
options: A. The object is speeding up steadily
B. The object is slowing down steadily
C. The object moves at constant velocity with zero acceleration
D. The object is at rest the whole time

questions.q_text: A car cruises at a steady twenty meters per second for eight seconds. Using the velocity-time graph idea, find its displacement.
questions.answer: Since the velocity is constant, the velocity-time graph is a flat line at twenty meters per second. The displacement equals the area between this line and the time axis, which is a rectangle. The area of a rectangle is height times width, so displacement equals velocity times time: twenty meters per second times eight seconds equals one hundred sixty meters. The car travels one hundred sixty meters.

questions.q_text: A car starts from rest and speeds up steadily, reaching a velocity of fifteen meters per second after ten seconds. Find both its acceleration and its displacement during these ten seconds.
questions.answer: First the acceleration: it is the slope of the line on the velocity-time graph. The velocity changes from zero to fifteen meters per second over ten seconds, so slope equals fifteen divided by ten, which is one point five meters per second every second. So the acceleration is one point five meters per second squared. Next the displacement: it is the area under the line. Because the car starts from rest and the line slopes straight up, the area is a triangle. The area of a triangle is one half times base times height: one half times ten seconds times fifteen meters per second equals seventy-five meters. So the displacement is seventy-five meters.

questions.q_text: A velocity-time graph shows a straight line sloping downward as an object slows to a stop. What does this indicate about the acceleration?
options: A. The acceleration is zero
B. The acceleration is positive and points along the velocity
C. The acceleration is negative, pointing opposite to the velocity
D. The acceleration increases steadily

questions.q_text: The three kinematic equations we discussed are only valid under one important condition. What is it?
options: A. The object must be at rest initially
B. The acceleration must be constant
C. The velocity must be constant
D. The displacement must be zero

questions.q_text: On a velocity-versus-time graph for motion with constant acceleration, what does the slope of the straight slanted line represent?
options: A. The displacement
B. The initial velocity
C. The acceleration
D. The total time

questions.q_text: Suppose you want to find the final velocity of a car given its initial velocity, acceleration, and the distance travelled, but you do NOT know the time. Which equation is most directly useful?
options: A. Final velocity equals initial velocity plus acceleration times time
B. Displacement equals initial velocity times time plus one half acceleration times time squared
C. Final velocity squared equals initial velocity squared plus two times acceleration times displacement
D. Displacement equals average velocity times time

questions.q_text: A car starts from rest and accelerates at a constant rate of 3 metres per second squared for 5 seconds. How fast is it going at the end, and how far has it travelled?
questions.answer: Step 1: List what we know. Initial velocity is 0 (starts from rest), acceleration is 3 metres per second squared, time is 5 seconds. Step 2: Find final velocity using the first equation: final velocity equals initial velocity plus acceleration times time. That is 0 plus 3 times 5, which equals 15 metres per second. Step 3: Find displacement using the second equation: displacement equals initial velocity times time plus one half times acceleration times time squared. That is 0 times 5, plus one half times 3 times 5 squared. Five squared is 25, half of 3 is 1.5, and 1.5 times 25 equals 37.5. So the displacement is 37.5 metres. Final answer: the car is moving at 15 metres per second and has travelled 37.5 metres.

questions.q_text: A motorcycle moving at 20 metres per second brakes with a constant acceleration of negative 4 metres per second squared until it stops. How far does it travel before stopping?
questions.answer: Step 1: List the knowns. Initial velocity is 20 metres per second, final velocity is 0 (it stops), acceleration is negative 4 metres per second squared. We do not know the time, so use the third equation. Step 2: Apply final velocity squared equals initial velocity squared plus two times acceleration times displacement. Substitute: 0 equals 20 squared plus 2 times negative 4 times displacement. Step 3: 20 squared is 400, and 2 times negative 4 is negative 8. So 0 equals 400 minus 8 times displacement. Step 4: Rearrange: 8 times displacement equals 400, so displacement equals 400 divided by 8, which is 50. Final answer: the motorcycle travels 50 metres before stopping.

questions.q_text: For an object moving back and forth along a straight line, what role do the plus and minus signs on velocity and displacement play?
options: A. They indicate the magnitude only
B. They indicate the direction of the motion
C. They indicate whether time is positive
D. They have no physical meaning

questions.q_text: What is the main reason motion in a plane is called two-dimensional motion?
options: A. Because it always happens at high speed
B. Because you need two directions to describe where the object is
C. Because two objects are always involved
D. Because it happens only on the ground

questions.q_text: Which of the following is the best example of motion in a plane?
options: A. A stone dropped straight down from a rooftop
B. A train moving along a straight track
C. A football kicked into the air, rising and curving forward before landing
D. An elevator moving straight up a building

questions.q_text: A car drives forward while also shifting sideways to overtake another car. How many directions are needed to fully describe its motion?
options: A. One direction is enough
B. Two directions are needed at the same time
C. Three directions are needed
D. No directions are needed

questions.q_text: According to the explanation, what happens to ideas like displacement and velocity when we move from one-dimensional to two-dimensional motion?
options: A. They are thrown away and replaced by new ideas
B. They stop being useful entirely
C. They stay the same but get richer, accounting for two directions at once
D. They only apply to circular motion

questions.q_text: For each of the following, decide whether it is one-dimensional (straight-line) motion or two-dimensional (motion in a plane), and briefly explain why: (1) a ball dropping straight down, (2) a satellite looping around the Earth, (3) a car moving steadily down a straight road, (4) a football kicked across a field into the air.
questions.answer:
Step 1: Recall the rule. If motion stays along a single straight line, only one direction is needed, so it is one-dimensional. If motion spreads across a flat surface and requires two directions at once, it is two-dimensional (motion in a plane).

Step 2: Examine each case.
(1) A ball dropping straight down moves only downward along one line, so only one direction is needed. This is one-dimensional motion.
(2) A satellite looping around the Earth follows a curved path, moving in two directions at once (it constantly changes direction across a surface), so this is two-dimensional motion in a plane.
(3) A car moving steadily down a straight road moves along a single line forward, needing only one direction. This is one-dimensional motion.
(4) A football kicked across a field rises (upward) and moves forward at the same time, tracing an arc. Two directions are involved, so this is two-dimensional motion in a plane.

Conclusion: Cases 1 and 3 are one-dimensional; cases 2 and 4 are two-dimensional.

questions.q_text: In uniform circular motion, the speed stays constant. What about the velocity?
options: A. The velocity is also constant because the speed never changes
B. The velocity keeps changing because its direction keeps changing
C. The velocity is zero at every point on the circle
D. The velocity changes only when the object slows down

questions.q_text: A runner goes around a circular track of radius 7 metres exactly once, taking 22 seconds to complete the loop. Take pi as 22/7. Find the average speed and the average velocity for this one complete loop.
questions.answer: Step 1: Find the distance travelled in one full loop. This equals the circumference of the circle, which is two times pi times the radius. So distance = 2 times (22/7) times 7 = 2 times 22 = 44 metres. Step 2: Average speed = distance divided by time = 44 metres divided by 22 seconds = 2 metres per second. Step 3: Find the displacement. After one complete loop, the runner ends at the same point where they started, so the displacement is zero. Step 4: Average velocity = displacement divided by time = 0 divided by 22 = 0. So the average speed is 2 metres per second, but the average velocity is zero.
